# Dealing with values the microscope cannot see {#sec-missing-data-measurement-error}

```{r}
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(brms)
library(posterior)
library(ggdist)
library(patchwork)
library(survival)
library(lme4)
library(glmmTMB)
library(mice)

# The book's shared plot theme (this also loads the legend helpers)
Plot_theme <- source("functions/plot_theme.R")
Plot_theme <- Plot_theme$value

# Okabe-Ito colors: two genotypes, and the three ways an attempt on the wire can end
col_geno <- c(WT = "#D55E00", KO = "#0072B2")
col_end <- c("Crossed" = "#999999", "Reached the cap" = "#D55E00", "Fell" = "#000000")

# Sampler settings for the multilevel fits
ml_control <- list(adapt_delta = 0.95)

# Median and 95% credible interval of a vector of draws, as text for the prose
qi <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  q <- unname(quantile(x, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE))
  sprintf("%s (95%% credible interval %s to %s)", round(q[1], digits), round(q[2], digits), round(q[3], digits))
}

# The same, in the short form "median [lower, upper]" for tables and tight sentences
qs <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  q <- unname(quantile(x, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE))
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f [%.", digits, "f, %.", digits, "f]"), q[1], q[2], q[3])
}

# Median and 95% limits of a vector of draws, as a one-row data frame for the forest plots
qrow <- function(x, label, group = NA) {
  q <- unname(quantile(x, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE))
  data.frame(label = label, group = group, med = q[1], lo = q[2], hi = q[3])
}
```

```{r}
#| label: prep-wire
#| include: false

# The hanging wire test: one row per mouse and day, three attempts per row (Klf4-KO and controls only)
wire_raw <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Wire_TrainingSum.csv"))
wire_raw <- wire_raw[wire_raw$Genotype %in% c("Klf4-KO", "WildType-Control"), ]

# One row per attempt, with the same codes as in the earlier chapters
attempts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(k) {
  data.frame(
    mouse = wire_raw$ReCode,
    genotype = factor(ifelse(wire_raw$Genotype == "Klf4-KO", "KO", "WT"), levels = c("WT", "KO")),
    day = wire_raw$Day,
    attempt = k,
    position = wire_raw[[paste0("Trial", k, "_Position")]],
    wire = wire_raw[[paste0("Trial", k, "_Wire")]],
    success = wire_raw[[paste0("Trial", k, "_Success")]]
  )
}))
attempts$mouse <- factor(attempts$mouse)
attempts$day_c <- attempts$day - 2
attempts$attempt_c <- attempts$attempt - 2

# How each attempt ended: the clock stops at 60 s (the cap), so a failure at 60 s is a timeout and a
# failure before 60 s is a fall. The two crossings recorded at exactly 60 s are flagged, not changed
attempts$end <- ifelse(attempts$success == 1, "Crossed", ifelse(attempts$wire >= 60, "Reached the cap", "Fell"))
attempts$end <- factor(attempts$end, levels = c("Crossed", "Reached the cap", "Fell"))
attempts$boundary <- attempts$success == 1 & attempts$wire >= 60

# The counts that I verified by hand against the file
stopifnot(nrow(attempts) == 567, sum(attempts$end != "Crossed") == 51, sum(attempts$end == "Reached the cap") == 45,
          sum(attempts$end == "Fell") == 6, sum(attempts$boundary) == 2)
n_att <- nrow(attempts)
n_mice_wire <- nlevels(attempts$mouse)
end_tab <- table(attempts$genotype, attempts$end)
n_by_geno <- table(attempts$genotype)

# The three mice with the most attempts that reached the cap
cap_by_mouse <- sort(table(attempts$mouse[attempts$end == "Reached the cap"]), decreasing = TRUE)
top3 <- names(cap_by_mouse)[1:3]
```

I have a spreadsheet row that I have looked at more often than I should. It is mouse `r top3[1]`, in the hanging wire test of @sec-beta-robust-regression, and `r cap_by_mouse[[1]]` of its nine attempts say the same thing: *60 seconds*. The next two mice on the list, `r top3[2]` and `r top3[3]`, have `r cap_by_mouse[[2]]` and `r cap_by_mouse[[3]]` of nine. Sixty seconds is not what those mice did. It is where the test stops: the experimenter takes the animal off the wire, the clock stops, and the row says 60. **How long would they have taken, if we had let them hang?** Nobody knows. What we know is that it was *more than 60*.

In earlier chapters I did the sensible-looking thing with those attempts and told you, each time, that I was not proud of it: I dropped them. The chapter on behavior (@sec-beta-robust-regression) modeled the completed crossing times only, the chapter on varying slopes (@sec-multilevel-varying-slopes) did the same, and the chapter on multilevel GLMs (@sec-multilevel-glmm) repaired the independence problem and left this one standing. Each time I wrote that the principled repair was a censored model and that it was a topic for this chapter. This is the chapter, and the first half of it pays that debt.

The second half is about values that are missing for other reasons. The chapters of this part set aside sections of brains that never made it into the file (@sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts), open-field sessions in which the tracker lost the mouse (@sec-longitudinal-timeseries), and a count whose error I mentioned and did not model (@sec-multivariate-distributional-regression). They are not the same problem as the 60-second cap, and I want to convince you that telling them apart is most of the work. @fig-mdme_attempts starts with the wire, because it is the case in which the missing values are on the page.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_attempts
#| fig-cap: "Every attempt of the 63 mice in the hanging wire test (567 attempts), by training day and genotype. Grey circles: the mouse crossed. Orange triangles: the attempt reached the 60-second cap, where the clock stops. Black crosses: the mouse fell before the cap. The dotted line is the cap. Points are jittered sideways within each day."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels, wild type on the left and Klf4-KO on the right, with training days 1, 2 and 3 on the horizontal axis and time on the wire in seconds from 0 to 60 on the vertical axis. Most points are grey circles between about 5 and 45 seconds. A row of orange triangles sits exactly on the dotted line at 60 seconds, a few in the wild-type panel and many more in the Klf4-KO panel on every day. Six black crosses, all in the Klf4-KO panel, lie between 12 and 32 seconds."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| warning: false

# Every attempt as a point; shape and color say how it ended, so the figure survives grayscale
set.seed(7)
ggplot(attempts, aes(x = day, y = wire, color = end, shape = end)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 60, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.22, height = 0, size = 1.9, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~genotype, labeller = labeller(genotype = c(WT = "Control", KO = "Klf4-KO"))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_end) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Crossed" = 16, "Reached the cap" = 17, "Fell" = 4)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3) +
  labs(x = "Training day", y = "Time on the wire (s)", color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_top()
```

I drew @fig-mdme_attempts with `ggplot2::geom_jitter()`, one mark per attempt, because with 567 attempts there is no reason to summarize before looking. A bar of mean crossing time per genotype, with asterisks, would be computed from the grey circles only (if you drop the rest) or would average the cap into the times as if the mice had really crossed at 60 (if you keep it), and in both cases it would hide the thing that is plainly visible here: a row of orange triangles that is a few marks long on the left and a crowd on the right, on every day. The design tip is to show *how each value ended*, not only its number, whenever a column mixes measurements with something else. Shape and color carry the same information, so it also reads in a grayscale print.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read the grey circles first: that is the part of the experiment that produced a time. Then find the dotted line and count the orange triangles sitting on it; they are not times, they are the places where we stopped looking. Compare the two panels *by the length of the row of triangles*, not by where the circles are, and notice that the row is longer on the right on all three days. Last, find the black crosses: they are a different event (a fall), and they are not triangles that happen to be early. The mistake to avoid is to read the height of an orange triangle as a measurement.
:::

## Three ways of not having the number {#sec-mdme-kinds}

There are, I think, three different reasons a number is not in your spreadsheet, and the habit I want you to leave with is asking *which one is it?* before touching any code. I picture them as three jars on a bench. In the first, the number is **absent**: the section was lost, the tracker lost the mouse, the animal did not survive the surgery. Something that could have been measured was not. In the second, the number is **hidden behind a limit**: the mouse was still hanging at 60 seconds, a western blot band is brighter than the film can record, a qPCR reaction did not cross the threshold. A measurement exists, and what we got back is only that it lies beyond a point. In the third, the number is **blurred**: the count of NeuN-positive cells in a region came from a microscope and a counting rule, and it carries a counting error that the spreadsheet does not show.

![Three jars on a bench, labeled by their contents and not by words. In the first, a few loose pieces and an empty slot: a number that is not there. In the second, a ruler that disappears into fog: a number that is only known to be beyond a point. In the third, a line drawn twice with a shaky hand: a number that is there, with some smear around it.](images/missing-data-measurement-error_three-jars.png){#fig-mdme-jars fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of three glass jars with cork lids on a wooden shelf. The first holds teal and ochre jigsaw pieces with one white gap among them. The second holds a wooden ruler standing upright whose marks are clear in the lower half and fade into pale teal fog above. The third holds a sheet with a teal line and an ochre line drawn side by side with a soft ochre smudge between them."}

@fig-mdme-jars is the map of the chapter: the first jar holds the number that is absent, the second the one hidden behind a limit and the third the one that is blurred, and the sections that follow take them in the order hidden, absent and blurred.

The three jars need different handling, and treating them alike is the commonest mistake I know. An absent value should be handled by asking why it is absent and by using a model that does not need it (or by saying what you assumed about it). A hidden value should *stay in the model*, with what we know about it, which is that it is beyond the limit. A blurred value should be modeled with its blur, which for a count has a known size. @tbl-mdme_kinds puts the three side by side with the case in this book that stands for each.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_kinds
#| tbl-cap: "Three ways of not having the number, what each assumes and what each costs, with the case of this chapter that stands for each one."

# One row per kind of missing value; the last column says what the book did with each case
kinds <- data.frame(
  Kind = c("Absent", "Hidden behind a limit", "Blurred"),
  `What we have` = c("Nothing for that unit (a section, a session, an animal)",
                     "That the value is at least (or at most) a limit",
                     "A value with a known amount of error"),
  `Tempting shortcut` = c("Drop the unit, or fill it with the group mean",
                          "Drop the unit, or replace it with the limit (or half the limit)",
                          "Treat the value as exact"),
  `What the shortcut costs` = c("Biased if the loss depends on the value; the lost units are not a random sample",
                                "Biased: dropping removes the slowest; replacing invents a value at the limit",
                                "Nothing if the error is small; attenuation and false precision if it is not"),
  `Better` = c("A model that uses what exists, and a sensitivity analysis for what cannot be checked",
               "A censored likelihood: the value contributes the probability of being beyond the limit",
               "A model that carries the error (a known standard error, or a count model with an offset)"),
  `Case in this chapter` = c("Open-field sessions, NeuN sections, one PDGFR-beta count",
                             "Attempts that reached the 60 s cap",
                             "NeuN counts"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(kinds)
```

Notice that the second row of @tbl-mdme_kinds is the one most scientists meet first and handle worst. A value below the limit of detection of an assay is replaced by half the limit, a time that reached the cap is entered as the cap, a band that saturated is entered at its maximum. Every one of those is a small act of invention, and the textbooks that this book follows are unanimous about it: dropping censored observations gives the wrong estimate, because what you drop is not a random subset, and substituting a constant creates a spike of identical values that shrinks the spread and distorts the slope [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. A reader of @sec-eda-missing-data will recognize the structure; this chapter is where the idea meets its second and third kinds.

## The mechanisms, on one page {#sec-mdme-mechanisms}

The vocabulary for absent values is the one of @sec-eda-missing-data, and I do not repeat the simulation that showed what each mechanism does to an estimate. I only need the three letters to be at hand. @tbl-mdme_mechanisms puts them next to the real cases of this chapter, and then I use the table for the rest of the chapter.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_mechanisms
#| tbl-cap: "The three missingness mechanisms of the earlier chapter, what a model that uses all the available data assumes under each, and the case of this chapter that I would place under it. The last column is a judgment from what I know of the experiments, not something the data can show."

# Mechanisms, what a likelihood-based analysis of the available data assumes, and the examples
mech <- data.frame(
  Mechanism = c("Missing completely at random (MCAR)", "Missing at random (MAR)", "Missing not at random (MNAR)"),
  `What it says` = c("The chance of being missing is unrelated to anything",
                     "The chance depends only on what is in the model (group, day, earlier values)",
                     "The chance depends on the missing value itself, after accounting for the model"),
  `Can the data tell?` = c("Partly: it can reject it, not confirm it",
                           "No: the missing values are the only evidence",
                           "No"),
  `A model with all the available data is` = c("Valid, and so is dropping rows (less efficient)",
                                                "Valid for the mean; dropping rows is not",
                                                "Biased; a model of the loss, or a sensitivity analysis, is needed"),
  `Where I would put the cases here` = c("A section lost to a cutting accident",
                                         "Mice that stop coming after a first session whose score is in the model",
                                         "A tracker that loses the mouse because of what the mouse does"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(mech)
```

Two sentences of that table carry most of what follows. The first is that **no analysis can show you that data are missing at random**, because the evidence against it sits in the values you do not have. The second is that, nevertheless, you can make the assumption *explicit and test how much the conclusion depends on it*, which is what a sensitivity analysis is. I will do the first thing for the wire, where the mechanism is known (the cap is a rule, so we know exactly what is censored), and the second for the open field, where it is not.

## Hidden behind a limit: the clock that stops at 60 seconds {#sec-mdme-wire}

Imagine a marathon in which the officials switch off the clock at four hours. You are given the finishing times and asked for the average. The runners who were still on the course are not in the list of times, and the average of the ones who finished is a number that tells you how long the race takes *for those who finish in under four hours*. It is not wrong as an arithmetic mean. It is wrong as an answer to the question that you were asked, which was about the runners, and it is wrong in a predictable direction: the slowest runners are exactly the ones that were dropped.

The wire is that marathon. @tbl-mdme_outcomes counts how the `r n_att` attempts ended, by genotype. `r end_tab["WT", "Reached the cap"]` of `r n_by_geno[["WT"]]` attempts of control mice reached the cap (`r round(100 * end_tab["WT", "Reached the cap"] / n_by_geno[["WT"]], 1)`%), against `r end_tab["KO", "Reached the cap"]` of `r n_by_geno[["KO"]]` of Klf4-KO mice (`r round(100 * end_tab["KO", "Reached the cap"] / n_by_geno[["KO"]], 1)`%), and the six falls are all in the knockouts.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_outcomes
#| tbl-cap: "How the 567 attempts of the hanging wire test ended, by genotype. The two crossings recorded at exactly 60 seconds are counted among the crossings."

# Counts and shares by genotype; the share not completed adds the cap and the falls
out_df <- data.frame(
  Genotype = c("Control", "Klf4-KO"),
  Attempts = as.integer(n_by_geno),
  Crossed = as.integer(end_tab[, "Crossed"]),
  `Reached the cap` = as.integer(end_tab[, "Reached the cap"]),
  Fell = as.integer(end_tab[, "Fell"]),
  `Not completed (%)` = round(100 * (end_tab[, "Reached the cap"] + end_tab[, "Fell"]) / as.integer(n_by_geno), 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(out_df)
```

I want the size of the problem in numbers before building anything. If I drop the failed attempts, I drop `r round(100 * (end_tab["WT", "Reached the cap"] + end_tab["WT", "Fell"]) / n_by_geno[["WT"]], 1)`% of the attempts of controls and `r round(100 * (end_tab["KO", "Reached the cap"] + end_tab["KO", "Fell"]) / n_by_geno[["KO"]], 1)`% of those of knockouts, which is `r round((end_tab["KO", "Reached the cap"] + end_tab["KO", "Fell"]) / n_by_geno[["KO"]] / ((end_tab["WT", "Reached the cap"] + end_tab["WT", "Fell"]) / n_by_geno[["WT"]]), 1)` times as many. The knockouts have the slowest mice, and they lose the most of their slowest attempts. A comparison of what is left compares a nearly complete set of control times with a trimmed set of knockout times, so it makes the knockouts look *less* different from controls than they are. The name for this, when the chance of being censored depends on the group or on the value, is [informative censoring]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. If the cap were an administrative accident that hit attempts at random (the experimenter had to leave at attempt 4), the censoring would be harmless to the comparison and the loss would only be a loss of information. Here the cap hits slowness, and slowness is what we are measuring [@harrell2015].

The case of one mouse shows it without a model. Mouse `r top3[1]` has `r cap_by_mouse[[1]]` attempts at the cap and `r sum(attempts$mouse == top3[1] & attempts$end == "Crossed")` completed ones, at `r paste(attempts$wire[attempts$mouse == top3[1] & attempts$end == "Crossed"], collapse = " and ")` seconds. The average of its completed attempts is `r round(mean(attempts$wire[attempts$mouse == top3[1] & attempts$end == "Crossed"]), 1)` seconds, which describes a quick mouse. Its average over all nine attempts is *at least* `r round(mean(attempts$wire[attempts$mouse == top3[1]]), 1)` seconds, because every attempt at the cap would have been 60 or more. The first number is what dropping reports; the second is the truth with a floor under it. A [censored]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} observation is exactly this: a measurement that we only know to be beyond a limit. When the limit is an upper one, as the 60-second cap, the observation is [right-censored]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}; when it is a lower one, as a value below the detection limit of an assay, it is [left-censored]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}. And a [truncated]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} observation is a different thing: a unit that is never in the sample at all if its value is beyond the limit, so that we do not even know it existed. Censored units are in the data with a bound; truncated units are not [@harrell2015].

![A wooden ruler that disappears into a bank of fog. We can read it up to the point where the fog begins, and after that we only know that the thing we are measuring is at least that long.](images/missing-data-measurement-error_ruler-into-fog.png){#fig-mdme-ruler fig-align="center" width="85%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a long wooden ruler lying on an off-white table, with clear tick marks on the left that fade into a bank of pale teal fog on the right, where the ruler is only a faint outline. A small white mouse stands at the edge of the fog, looking up into it."}

@fig-mdme-ruler is the whole idea of censoring in one picture: up to the fog the marks tell us how long the thing is, and beyond it we only know that it is at least that long.

### Every attempt, accounted for {#sec-mdme-km}

Before any model, I want a picture in which *no attempt is dropped and none is invented*. The question that fits the data is not "what was the time?" but "by second *t*, what share of the attempts had not yet been completed?". That is a [survival curve]{.ix ix="survival curve"} in the language of time-to-event analysis (the share still "surviving", here still on the wire at time *t*), estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method [@kaplan1958], and it handles a censored attempt in the only honest way: it stays in the denominator until the moment its clock stops, and leaves then. I use `survival::survfit()` [@survival] and draw the steps with `ggplot2::geom_step()` and a ribbon for the 95% confidence interval. A bar plot of mean times would give one number per genotype; this curve gives every second of the test, and it shows where the two groups separate and what is left at the end.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_km
#| fig-cap: "Share of attempts not yet completed at each second of the hanging wire test, by genotype (Kaplan-Meier estimate with 95% confidence interval). Every one of the 567 attempts is used: attempts that reach the cap stay in the denominator until 60 seconds, and the six falls (crosses) leave at the moment they fell. The dotted line is the cap."
#| fig-alt: "Two descending step curves from 1 at time 0. The orange curve (control) falls steeply to about 0.28 at 20 seconds and to about 0.04 at 60 seconds. The blue curve (Klf4-KO) falls more slowly, to about 0.58 at 20 seconds, 0.32 at 30 seconds and 0.12 at 60 seconds. Both curves stay flat after 60 seconds, which is the cap, marked with a dotted vertical line. Six small black crosses sit on the blue curve between 12 and 32 seconds."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| warning: false

# Time to cross: an attempt that crossed is an event; the rest leave the risk set when their clock stops
km_dat <- attempts
km_dat$time <- pmax(km_dat$wire, 0.5)
km_dat$event <- as.numeric(km_dat$end == "Crossed")
sf <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ genotype, data = km_dat)

# Steps of each curve, with the starting point at time 0
sf_df <- data.frame(time = sf$time, surv = sf$surv, lo = sf$lower, hi = sf$upper,
                    genotype = rep(c("WT", "KO"), sf$strata))
sf_df <- rbind(sf_df, data.frame(time = 0, surv = 1, lo = 1, hi = 1, genotype = c("WT", "KO")))

# Height of the curve at the moment each fall happened (the crosses)
fall_df <- attempts[attempts$end == "Fell", c("genotype", "wire")]
fall_df$surv <- NA
for (i in seq_len(nrow(fall_df))) {
  s <- sf_df[sf_df$genotype == fall_df$genotype[i], ]
  s <- s[order(s$time), ]
  fall_df$surv[i] <- tail(s$surv[s$time <= fall_df$wire[i]], 1)
}

# Share still hanging when the clock stops, for the labels on the right
end_surv <- sapply(c("WT", "KO"), function(g) min(sf_df$surv[sf_df$genotype == g]))

# Curves, ribbons, direct labels, the cap, and the falls
ggplot(sf_df, aes(x = time, y = surv, color = genotype, fill = genotype)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), stat = "identity", alpha = 0.15, colour = NA, outline.type = "full") +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(data = fall_df, aes(x = wire, y = surv), shape = 4, size = 3, stroke = 1.2, color = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = 36, y = 0.50, label = "Klf4-KO", color = col_geno[["KO"]], fontface = "bold", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 24, y = 0.12, label = "Control", color = col_geno[["WT"]], fontface = "bold", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 59, y = 0.60, label = "cap", hjust = 1, size = 4.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_geno) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_geno) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 15, 30, 45, 60)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 62)) +
  labs(x = "Time on the wire (s)", y = "Share of attempts not yet completed") +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_none()
```

I read the picture in three steps, and this is how I would teach you to read any curve of this kind.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
The vertical axis is the share of attempts still *not completed* at the second on the horizontal axis, so every curve starts at 1 and can only go down. First look at how fast each curve falls: a curve that falls early is a group that crosses quickly. Then look at the height of the curve at the dotted line. That height is the share of attempts that were still hanging when the clock stopped, which is the censored share, and here it is `r round(100 * end_surv[["WT"]], 1)`% for controls and `r round(100 * end_surv[["KO"]], 1)`% for knockouts. Last, notice that the curves are flat after 60: the test says nothing about what would have happened, so the flat part is not a prediction. The mistake to avoid is to read the plateau as "these mice never cross"; it says "we stopped looking".
:::

The two curves tell the story of the chapter before I fit anything. The knockouts' curve is above the controls' at every second, which is what a slower group looks like, and it ends at a plateau about `r round(end_surv[["KO"]] / end_surv[["WT"]], 1)` times as high. The model I build next is a way of putting that picture into one number (a ratio of typical crossing times) *without* throwing away the attempts that make the plateau.

### Two things that are not censored times {#sec-mdme-falls}

Two groups of attempts need a decision before the model, and I made the rule first and checked it in code, as I did with the impossible record in @sec-beta-robust-regression. The first group is the six **falls**. A mouse that falls at 12 seconds has not been stopped by the cap. It has had a different event, and what its "time to cross" would have been had it stayed on is a counterfactual that I do not know how to fill in; it is not "at least 12 seconds" in the way that a timeout is "at least 60", because falling may itself be related to how hard the crossing was. All six are in knockout mice, on days 1 to 3 (@tbl-mdme_falls).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_falls
#| tbl-cap: "The six attempts that ended in a fall before the cap, and the two crossings recorded at exactly 60 seconds. Times in seconds; position is the time to get into position."

# The two kinds of attempt that are not an ordinary crossing or a timeout
odd <- attempts[attempts$end == "Fell" | attempts$boundary, c("mouse", "genotype", "day", "attempt", "position", "wire", "end")]
odd$end <- ifelse(odd$end == "Fell", "Fell", "Crossed at exactly 60 s")
names(odd) <- c("Mouse", "Genotype", "Day", "Attempt", "Position", "Time", "How it ended")
knitr::kable(odd[order(odd$`How it ended`, odd$Mouse), ], row.names = FALSE)
```

My rule for the main analysis is therefore: **falls are not censored times, and they are left out of the model of the crossing time**; they are counted, reported (6 of 315 attempts of knockouts, none in controls), and shown with their own sensitivity analysis below, in which they are treated in the two ways that bracket the possibilities. The second group is the two crossings recorded at exactly 60 seconds. Daniel confirmed that these mice reached the platform in the last second, so they are real crossings and I keep them as exact times of 60 s; the cost of being wrong is small and I tested it, by refitting with both of them recoded as censored. They are the kind of boundary case that is only visible because I looked for values that sit on a limit.

### The censored model {#sec-mdme-censmodel}

The model is the Student-*t* of @sec-beta-robust-regression on the log of the time, with the varying intercept for each mouse of @sec-multilevel-glmm, and one change in the likelihood. For an attempt that was completed, the likelihood contribution is the height of the density at the observed log time, as always. For an attempt that reached the cap, I do not have a log time; what I have is that the log time was *larger than* $\log 60$, and the contribution is the probability of that, the area under the density beyond the cap (@eq-mdme-cens). The mouse that hit the cap contributes less than a mouse that crossed, because it tells us less, but it contributes in the right direction.

$$
L_i = \begin{cases}
f\left(\log y_i \mid \mu_i, \sigma, \nu\right) & \text{if the attempt was completed}\\[4pt]
1 - F\left(\log 60 \mid \mu_i, \sigma, \nu\right) & \text{if it reached the cap}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-mdme-cens}

with $f$ and $F$ the density and the cumulative distribution function of the Student-*t* and $\mu_i$ the linear predictor of @sec-multilevel-glmm: genotype, day and attempt, plus a level for the mouse. In `brms` the only change is the left side of the formula: `log_wire | cens(cens)`, where `cens` says for each row whether the value is exact (`"none"`) or a lower bound (`"right"`). The priors are those of @sec-multilevel-glmm (`Normal(3, 0.7)` for the intercept on the log scale, `Normal(0, 0.5)` for coefficients, `Exponential(2)` for the scale, `Gamma(2, 0.1)` for the degrees of freedom and `Exponential(3)` for the spread between mice), so that the *only* thing that changes is what I do with the censored attempts. I fit that model and the alternatives that I want to compare it with: the Gaussian of the first chapter on behavior (completed attempts, independent), the Student-*t* with a level for mouse on completed attempts only (the model of @sec-multilevel-glmm), and the Student-*t* in which the capped attempts are entered as exact times of 60 seconds (the replacement that I warned you about).

```{r}
#| label: prep-wire-fits
#| include: false

# Data for each analysis. Completed attempts: log time. Censored: reached the cap, log(60) is a lower bound.
# Falls are excluded from the main data (their own sensitivity analysis follows)
wire_done <- attempts[attempts$end == "Crossed" & attempts$wire > 0, ]
wire_done$log_wire <- log(wire_done$wire)

wire_all <- attempts[attempts$end != "Fell", ]
wire_all$log_wire <- log(wire_all$wire)
wire_all$cens <- ifelse(wire_all$end == "Reached the cap", "right", "none")

# Replacement: the capped attempts entered as exact times of 60 seconds
wire_subst <- wire_all
wire_subst$cens <- "none"

# Falls censored at the moment they fell (a fall as "we stopped watching"), and falls treated as if
# they had reached the cap (the bracketing worst case)
wire_fall_t <- attempts
wire_fall_t$log_wire <- log(pmax(wire_fall_t$wire, 0.5))
wire_fall_t$cens <- ifelse(wire_fall_t$end == "Crossed", "none", "right")
wire_fall_cap <- wire_fall_t
wire_fall_cap$log_wire[wire_fall_cap$end == "Fell"] <- log(60)

# The two crossings at exactly 60 s recoded as censored
wire_bound <- wire_all
wire_bound$cens[wire_bound$boundary] <- "right"

# Priors: those of the multilevel chapter, so that only the treatment of the capped attempts changes
prior_gauss <- c(prior(normal(3, 0.7), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
                 prior(exponential(2), class = "sigma"))
prior_t <- c(prior_gauss, prior(gamma(2, 0.1), class = "nu"))
prior_t_ml <- c(prior_t, prior(exponential(3), class = "sd"))
prior_t_ml_narrow <- c(prior(normal(3, 0.7), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 0.25), class = "b"),
                       prior(exponential(2), class = "sigma"), prior(gamma(2, 0.2), class = "nu"),
                       prior(exponential(6), class = "sd"))
prior_t_ml_wide <- c(prior(normal(3, 0.7), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
                     prior(exponential(2), class = "sigma"), prior(gamma(2, 0.05), class = "nu"),
                     prior(exponential(1), class = "sd"))
# Logistic model for "not completed": as in the multilevel chapter (log-odds)
prior_logit <- c(prior(normal(-2, 1.5), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"),
                 prior(exponential(0.5), class = "sd"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fit-wire-cens

# 1. Gaussian on completed attempts, attempts treated as independent
fit_w1 <- brm(
  log_wire ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c,
  data = wire_done, family = gaussian(), prior = prior_gauss,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit1.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 2. Student-t with a level for each mouse, completed attempts only (the model of the multilevel chapter)
fit_w2 <- brm(
  log_wire ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_done, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit2.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 3. The same, with the capped attempts entered as exact times of 60 seconds
fit_w3 <- brm(
  log_wire ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_subst, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit3.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 4. The censored model: capped attempts contribute the probability of being beyond 60 seconds
fit_w4 <- brm(
  log_wire | cens(cens) ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_all, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit4.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
# Population effects, spread between mice, residual scale and degrees of freedom of the censored model
summary(fit_w4)
```

### survival

```{r}
# The frequentist counterpart: a censored lognormal model with standard errors that allow for the mouse
sr_dat <- wire_all
sr_dat$event <- as.numeric(sr_dat$cens == "none")
survreg_w <- survreg(Surv(wire, event) ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + cluster(mouse),
                     data = sr_dat, dist = "lognormal")
summary(survreg_w)
```
:::

The coefficients are on the log scale, so I read them as ratios. `genotypeKO` is the log of the ratio of the *typical* (median) crossing time of a knockout mouse to that of a control mouse at the same day and attempt, and `day_c` is the log of the ratio for one more day of training. Before reading them I check the sampler: the censored fit has a maximum R-hat of `r round(max(summarise_draws(as_draws_df(fit_w4), "rhat")$rhat, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` and its smallest effective sample size is `r round(min(summarise_draws(as_draws_df(fit_w4), "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")[, 2:3], na.rm = TRUE))`; the full table is in @sec-mdme-checks.

```{r}
#| label: draws-wire
#| include: false

# Posterior draws of the four models and the maximum-likelihood estimate of the frequentist one
dr_w <- lapply(list(w1 = fit_w1, w2 = fit_w2, w3 = fit_w3, w4 = fit_w4), as_draws_df)
sr_b <- coef(survreg_w)["genotypeKO"]
sr_se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(survreg_w)))["genotypeKO"]
ratio_ko <- exp(dr_w$w4$b_genotypeKO)
ratio_day <- exp(dr_w$w4$b_day_c)
```

### Dropping, replacing, censoring {#sec-mdme-compare}

@fig-mdme_wire_forest puts the three treatments of the capped attempts side by side, and then adds the sensitivity analyses that I describe below. The effect is the ratio of the typical crossing time of a knockout mouse to that of a control mouse. I drew it as a forest of intervals on adjacent rows, as in @sec-multilevel-glmm, because what I want you to see is the *position* of the estimates, not their significance: a bar chart of three coefficients with stars would tell you that all three "are significant" and nothing about the fact that two of them are biased.

```{r}
#| label: fit-wire-sens

# 5. Falls censored at the moment they fell (cause-specific view)
fit_w5 <- brm(
  log_wire | cens(cens) ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_fall_t, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit5.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 6. Falls treated as if they had reached the cap (worst case for the knockouts)
fit_w6 <- brm(
  log_wire | cens(cens) ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_fall_cap, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit6.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 7. The two crossings at exactly 60 s recoded as censored
fit_w7 <- brm(
  log_wire | cens(cens) ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_bound, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit7.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 8 and 9. Prior sensitivity of the censored model: a narrower and a wider set of priors
fit_w8 <- brm(
  log_wire | cens(cens) ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_all, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml_narrow,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit8.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
fit_w9 <- brm(
  log_wire | cens(cens) ~ genotype + day_c + attempt_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = wire_all, family = student(), prior = prior_t_ml_wide,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit9.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_wire_forest
#| fig-cap: "Ratio of the typical crossing time of Klf4-KO mice to that of control mice, under different treatments of the attempts that did not produce a time. Points are posterior medians (the frequentist estimate in the last row); bars are 95% intervals. The dotted line is a ratio of 1 (no difference). The top three rows differ only in what is done with the 45 attempts that reached the cap; the next three are sensitivity analyses of the censored model."
#| fig-alt: "A forest plot with eight rows and a logarithmic horizontal axis from 1 to 1.8. The first two rows, a Gaussian model and a Student-t model on completed attempts, have points at about 1.28, with intervals from about 1.18 to 1.39 (Gaussian, attempts independent) and from about 1.08 to 1.51 (Student-t with mouse levels). The third row, with the capped attempts entered as 60 seconds, is at about 1.40. The fourth row, the censored model, is at about 1.44 with an interval from about 1.13 to 1.80. Three sensitivity rows (falls censored at the moment of the fall, falls treated as reaching the cap, the two 60-second crossings as censored) lie at about 1.43 to 1.46, and the last row, the frequentist survival model, is at about 1.41."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| warning: false

# Ratios and intervals of the genotype effect under each treatment
dr_w$w5 <- as_draws_df(fit_w5); dr_w$w6 <- as_draws_df(fit_w6); dr_w$w7 <- as_draws_df(fit_w7)
forest_w <- rbind(
  qrow(exp(dr_w$w1$b_genotypeKO), "Gaussian, completed only, independent", "Drop"),
  qrow(exp(dr_w$w2$b_genotypeKO), "Student-t + mouse levels, completed only", "Drop"),
  qrow(exp(dr_w$w3$b_genotypeKO), "Student-t, cap entered as 60 s", "Replace"),
  qrow(exp(dr_w$w4$b_genotypeKO), "Censored Student-t (main model)", "Censor"),
  qrow(exp(dr_w$w5$b_genotypeKO), "Censored, falls censored when they fell", "Sensitivity"),
  qrow(exp(dr_w$w6$b_genotypeKO), "Censored, falls as reaching the cap", "Sensitivity"),
  qrow(exp(dr_w$w7$b_genotypeKO), "Censored, two 60 s crossings censored", "Sensitivity")
)
forest_w <- rbind(forest_w, data.frame(label = "survreg (lognormal, robust SE)", group = "Frequentist",
                                       med = exp(sr_b), lo = exp(sr_b - 1.96 * sr_se), hi = exp(sr_b + 1.96 * sr_se)))
forest_w$label <- factor(forest_w$label, levels = rev(forest_w$label))
forest_w$group <- factor(forest_w$group, levels = c("Drop", "Replace", "Censor", "Sensitivity", "Frequentist"))

# Points with 95% intervals on a ratio scale, one row per analysis
ggplot(forest_w, aes(x = med, y = label, xmin = lo, xmax = hi, color = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.55, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 1.25, 1.5, 2)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Drop" = "#999999", "Replace" = "#E69F00", "Censor" = "#0072B2",
                                "Sensitivity" = "#56B4E9", "Frequentist" = "#000000")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Drop" = 16, "Replace" = 15, "Censor" = 17, "Sensitivity" = 17, "Frequentist" = 18)) +
  labs(x = "Ratio of typical times, KO to control (log scale)", y = NULL, color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  legend_none() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11))
```

@fig-mdme_wire_forest has one message and one caution. The message: **dropping the capped attempts makes the knockout delay look smaller** (a ratio of `r qs(exp(dr_w$w1$b_genotypeKO), 2)` with the Gaussian of the chapter on behavior and `r qs(exp(dr_w$w2$b_genotypeKO), 2)` with the Student-*t* on completed attempts with a level for each mouse), the replacement gets closer (`r qs(exp(dr_w$w3$b_genotypeKO), 2)`), since a 60 is at least a lower bound of the truth, but it invents a value and gives it the weight of a measurement, and the censored model says `r qs(ratio_ko, 2)`: the typical crossing of a knockout takes `r round(100 * (median(ratio_ko) - 1))`% longer than that of a control, not `r round(100 * (median(exp(dr_w$w2$b_genotypeKO)) - 1))`%. The direction is the one I predicted from @tbl-mdme_outcomes. The caution is about *how much*: the censored interval is wider than the interval of the models that dropped attempts, and it should be, because it admits that `r sum(wire_all$cens == "right")` of the attempts told us only a bound. A narrower interval from a model that discards the hardest attempts is not a better result; it is a more confident answer to an easier question.

Three sensitivity analyses sit below the main row. The two about the falls bracket what a fall could mean: if a fall is just "we stopped watching" the ratio is `r qs(exp(dr_w$w5$b_genotypeKO), 2)`, and if a fall is as bad as reaching the cap (every mouse that fell would have hung on until the end) it is `r qs(exp(dr_w$w6$b_genotypeKO), 2)`. Six attempts out of `r n_att` do not decide the conclusion, and the figure says so. Recoding the two crossings at exactly 60 seconds as censored gives `r qs(exp(dr_w$w7$b_genotypeKO), 2)`. And the frequentist estimate from `survival::survreg()` is `r round(exp(sr_b), 2)` (95% confidence interval `r round(exp(sr_b - 1.96 * sr_se), 2)` to `r round(exp(sr_b + 1.96 * sr_se), 2)`).

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`survreg()` fits the censored model by maximum likelihood, with a lognormal distribution for the time (a Gaussian on the log scale) instead of the Student-*t*, and with standard errors that allow for the clustering of attempts within mice (`cluster(mouse)`). That is not the same model as the `brms` one: it has no varying intercept, so the mouse-to-mouse variation enters only through the standard error, and its tails are those of a Gaussian. The agreement of the point estimate with the censored `brms` model (`r round(exp(sr_b), 2)` against `r round(median(ratio_ko), 2)`) is the reassuring part: the censored likelihood is doing the work, in both. Where they differ is in the width of the interval and in how they treat mice: `brms` estimates the spread between mice and shrinks each mouse toward its genotype; `survreg()` ignores that structure and corrects the standard error afterwards. `parsnip`, which the book used for the simple models, has no engine for a censored regression with a varying intercept, and `survreg()` in `survival` [@therneau2000] does not support random effects (I tried a Gaussian frailty term and it is refused). A Cox model with a random intercept exists in the `coxme` [@coxme] package, but it answers a different question (a ratio of hazards, not of times) and belongs to the appendix on time-to-event models (@sec-appendix-next), which I do not enter.
:::

### The other view: the probability of not completing {#sec-mdme-logit}

Everything so far is about *how long* a crossing takes. The other question the data can answer is *whether* it happens, and it is the one that does not need any assumption about the values behind the cap. I model the probability that an attempt is not completed (reaches the cap or falls) with the logistic model with a varying intercept of @sec-multilevel-glmm, and I report it two ways, as an odds ratio for a typical mouse and as the average difference in probability over the mice we studied (@sec-glmm-marginal).

```{r}
#| label: fit-wire-logit

# Not completed (cap or fall) as a yes/no, with a level for each mouse
attempts$failed <- 1 - attempts$success
fit_w10 <- brm(
  failed ~ genotype + day_c + (1 | mouse),
  data = attempts, family = bernoulli(), prior = prior_logit,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 4000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit10.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
dr_l <- as_draws_df(fit_w10)

# Average predictive comparison: every attempt as if by a knockout and as if by a control
nd_ko <- attempts; nd_ko$genotype <- factor("KO", levels = c("WT", "KO"))
nd_wt <- attempts; nd_wt$genotype <- factor("WT", levels = c("WT", "KO"))
p_ko <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(fit_w10, newdata = nd_ko))
p_wt <- rowMeans(posterior_epred(fit_w10, newdata = nd_wt))
```

For a typical mouse the odds of not completing an attempt are `r qs(exp(dr_l$b_genotypeKO), 1)` times as large in knockouts as in controls; averaged over the mice of the experiment, the probability of not completing an attempt is `r qs(100 * p_ko, 1)`% for knockouts against `r qs(100 * p_wt, 1)`% for controls, a difference of `r qs(100 * (p_ko - p_wt), 1)` percentage points. This view and the censored model agree about the direction and about the group that is in trouble, and they do so for different reasons: the logistic model uses only whether the attempt ended at all, and the censored model uses *also* how close to the cap the completed attempts were. Reporting both is not redundancy. A reader who distrusts the tail assumption of the censored model can fall back on the probability, and a reader who wants the time can have it.

### Does the censored model reproduce the cap? {#sec-mdme-ppc}

A model for a limit should, at the least, reproduce *how often the limit is reached*. I check it by simulating, from the censored model, a new time for every attempt and counting how often the simulated time is above 60 seconds, by genotype and day, against the observed share of attempts at the cap (@fig-mdme_wire_ppc). It is the predictive check of @sec-mcmc-model-checking, with a statistic chosen for the problem: the share beyond the cap, because the cap is exactly what this chapter is about.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_wire_ppc
#| fig-cap: "Share of attempts that reached the cap, by genotype and day: observed (black points) and expected under the censored model (blue points and lines are the median and 95% interval of the simulated share). Mice are those of the experiment, so the check is on the fitted mice."
#| fig-alt: "Six groups of points along days 1, 2 and 3 in two panels, control on the left and Klf4-KO on the right. Black points show the observed share of attempts at the cap, about 1 to 6% in controls and about 10 to 15% in knockouts. Blue points with vertical lines show the model's expected share, close to the black points in every group, with intervals that contain them."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| warning: false

# Simulate a new log time for every analyzed attempt and flag the ones beyond the cap
set.seed(11)
yrep <- posterior_predict(fit_w4, ndraws = 500)
beyond <- yrep > log(60)
grp <- interaction(wire_all$genotype, wire_all$day, drop = TRUE)
pp_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(grp), function(g) {
  idx <- which(grp == g)
  share <- rowMeans(beyond[, idx, drop = FALSE])
  data.frame(genotype = wire_all$genotype[idx[1]], day = wire_all$day[idx[1]],
             obs = mean(wire_all$end[idx] == "Reached the cap"),
             med = median(share), lo = quantile(share, 0.025), hi = quantile(share, 0.975))
}))

# Observed share against the model's band
ggplot(pp_df, aes(x = day)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(y = med, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), color = "#0072B2", size = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = obs), color = "black", size = 2.6, shape = 15) +
  facet_wrap(~genotype, labeller = labeller(genotype = c(WT = "Control", KO = "Klf4-KO"))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Training day", y = "Share of attempts beyond 60 s") +
  Plot_theme
```

The black squares of @fig-mdme_wire_ppc sit inside the bands for `r sum(pp_df$obs >= pp_df$lo & pp_df$obs <= pp_df$hi)` of the `r nrow(pp_df)` groups, and above the median of the band in `r sum(pp_df$obs > pp_df$med)` of them: the model reproduces the share at the cap on day 1, but it **under-predicts it on days 2 and 3**, most clearly for the knockouts on day 3 (observed `r round(100 * pp_df$obs[pp_df$genotype == "KO" & pp_df$day == 3])`%, expected `r round(100 * pp_df$med[pp_df$genotype == "KO" & pp_df$day == 3])`%). The reason is visible in @fig-mdme_attempts: the crossing times fall by about a fifth per day, and the model carries that practice effect into the tail, so that it expects fewer attempts at the cap as the days go by, whereas the share of attempts at the cap in the knockouts hardly moves (`r paste0(round(100 * pp_df$obs[pp_df$genotype == "KO"]), "%", collapse = ", ")` on days 1 to 3). Mice that reach the cap do not seem to be simply slow versions of mice that cross: for some attempts something else is going on, and a single distribution of times describes that only approximately. I do not think this undoes the comparison of typical times, which is dominated by the 516 crossings, but it is a limit of the model and I would say so in a paper; it is also the reason for reporting the probability of not completing an attempt next to the ratio of times, as above. The check cannot say anything about the shape of the tail beyond 60 seconds, since there are no data beyond 60. That part is an assumption, and the table of prior sensitivity in @sec-mdme-checks is where I look at how much it matters.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results.** Of `r n_att` attempts by `r n_mice_wire` mice, `r end_tab["WT", "Reached the cap"]` of `r n_by_geno[["WT"]]` attempts of control mice and `r end_tab["KO", "Reached the cap"]` of `r n_by_geno[["KO"]]` of Klf4-KO mice reached the 60-second limit of the test, and 6 attempts, all by knockouts, ended in a fall. Treating the limit as a right-censored time, the typical crossing time of Klf4-KO mice was `r qs(ratio_ko, 2)` times that of controls (posterior median and 95% credible interval; a posterior probability above `r floor(100 * mean(ratio_ko > 1))`% that the ratio exceeds 1), against `r qs(exp(dr_w$w2$b_genotypeKO), 2)` when the capped attempts were omitted. Each day of training reduced crossing times by a factor of `r qs(ratio_day, 2)`. The probability of not completing an attempt was `r qs(100 * p_ko, 1)`% in knockouts and `r qs(100 * p_wt, 1)`% in controls, and it did not fall with training in knockouts, which the time model does not reproduce.

**Methods.** The log of the time on the wire was modeled with a Student-*t* likelihood, with genotype, day and attempt as predictors and a varying intercept for each mouse. Attempts that reached the 60-second limit were treated as right-censored at 60 s; falls (6 attempts) were excluded from the time model and analyzed in sensitivity analyses in which they were censored at the time of the fall or treated as reaching the limit. The model was fitted in `brms` (four chains of 3,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 for all parameters). The estimate assumes that the log times beyond 60 s follow the same Student-*t* distribution as the observed ones; the model under-predicted the share of attempts at the limit on days 2 and 3.
:::

## Absent: sessions and sections that are not there {#sec-mdme-absent}

The wire was the easy case, in one sense: the mechanism is a rule that I can read in the lab manual, so I know exactly which values are censored and by how much. The absent values of the rest of this part are harder, because nobody wrote a rule for them. A tracker loses a mouse; a section is damaged on the cryostat; an animal does not wake up from the surgery. For each of them I can ask three questions, and the order matters: *what is missing, why do I think it is missing, and what would change my mind?*

### The open-field sessions that the tracker lost {#sec-mdme-of}

The open-field data are those of @sec-beta-robust-regression and @sec-longitudinal-timeseries, and I do not reopen any of their decisions: the animal is identified by the `Animal` column, animals whose treatment label changes between days are left out, the outcome is the share of the *tracked* time spent in the center, and a session needs at least 270 of its 300 seconds tracked. The rule of 270 seconds was inherited, not chosen, and the chapter on longitudinal models refit the model without it and said that the conclusion did not depend on where the line was drawn. Here I want to look at *what the rule removed*.

```{r}
#| label: data-openfield

# Read the open-field summary as it came (column names contain spaces and colons)
of_raw <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/OpenField_Summary.csv"), check.names = FALSE)

# One row per animal and test day; times in seconds. The animal is identified by Animal, not by ReCode
of <- data.frame(
  animal = sub("^0+", "", sub("^M", "", of_raw$Animal)),
  label = of_raw$Treatment,
  dpi = of_raw$DPI,
  center = of_raw[["Center : time"]],
  arena = of_raw[["Arena : time"]],
  borders = of_raw[["Borders : time"]]
)
of$tracked <- of$center + of$arena + of$borders

# Animals whose treatment label changes between days are excluded, as in the earlier chapters
labels_per <- tapply(of$label, of$animal, function(z) length(unique(z)))
bad_animals <- names(which(labels_per > 1))
groups4 <- c("WildType", "WT-Sham", "Klf4-KO", "KO-Sham")
of4 <- of[!(of$animal %in% bad_animals) & of$label %in% groups4 & of$tracked > 0, ]

# The four groups of the earlier chapters; the share of tracked time in the center; short = under 270 s
of4$genotype <- factor(ifelse(grepl("KO", of4$label), "KO", "WT"), levels = c("WT", "KO"))
of4$surgery <- factor(ifelse(grepl("Sham", of4$label), "sham", "ischemia"), levels = c("sham", "ischemia"))
of4$group <- factor(paste(of4$genotype, of4$surgery), levels = c("WT sham", "WT ischemia", "KO sham", "KO ischemia"))
of4$share <- of4$center / of4$tracked
of4$short <- of4$tracked < 270
of4$dpi_f <- factor(of4$dpi)
of4$animal <- factor(of4$animal)

# The counts of the earlier chapters: 48 animals, 38 of them with a session on day 1 that meets the rule
stopifnot(length(unique(of4$animal)) == 48, sum(of4$dpi == 1 & !of4$short) == 38)
n_of_an <- nlevels(of4$animal)
n_of_sess <- nrow(of4)
n_short <- sum(of4$short)
n_absent <- 6 * n_of_an - n_of_sess
d1 <- of4[of4$dpi == 1, ]
```

There are `r n_of_an` animals in the four groups, `r 6 * n_of_an` possible sessions (six days each) and `r n_of_sess` sessions in the file: `r n_absent` are absent altogether, and of the ones that exist, `r n_short` have fewer than 270 tracked seconds (@fig-lt_missing of @sec-longitudinal-timeseries draws the grid). The rule drops those `r n_short`. Day 1 is the day that matters, because it is the one day on which the ischemic animals differ from the shams, and it is also the day with the most lost sessions: `r sum(d1$short)` of `r nrow(d1)`. Whether those sessions are a random sample of day-1 sessions is a question the data can partly answer, because *the lost sessions were not lost entirely*: the tracker followed the mouse for some of the five minutes, and the share of that tracked time in the center is in the file.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_of_lost
#| fig-cap: "Day 1 of the open field. Left: the share of tracked time in the center for every session, by group; filled circles are sessions with at least 270 tracked seconds (kept by the rule) and open triangles are sessions with less. Right: the same share against the seconds tracked, for all days and groups (log scale for the share; sessions with no time in the center are not shown)."
#| fig-alt: "Left panel: four groups on the horizontal axis (control sham, control ischemia, Klf4-KO sham, Klf4-KO ischemia) and the share of time in the center on the vertical axis from 0 to 0.95. Filled circles in the two ischemia groups spread from near zero to 0.93, with a median around 0.1 to 0.2. Open triangles for sessions that were lost sit low, mostly under 0.15. Right panel: share of tracked time in the center on a logarithmic axis against tracked seconds from 0 to 300; the open triangles with fewer than 270 tracked seconds lie in the lower part of the cloud."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| warning: false

# Left: every day-1 session; the lost ones are drawn open and labeled with the seconds that were tracked
set.seed(5)
pA <- ggplot(d1, aes(x = group, y = share, shape = short, color = short)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.18, height = 0, size = 2.2, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 16, "TRUE" = 2), labels = c("FALSE" = "270 s or more (kept)", "TRUE" = "under 270 s (lost)")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#0072B2", "TRUE" = "#D55E00"), labels = c("FALSE" = "270 s or more (kept)", "TRUE" = "under 270 s (lost)")) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("WT sham" = "Control\nsham", "WT ischemia" = "Control\nischemia", "KO sham" = "KO\nsham", "KO ischemia" = "KO\nischemia")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of tracked time in the center", shape = NULL, color = NULL) +
  Plot_theme + legend_inside(0.5, 0.9) + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12))

# Right: all sessions, share against the seconds tracked
pB <- ggplot(of4[of4$share > 0, ], aes(x = tracked, y = share, shape = short, color = short)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 16, "TRUE" = 2)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#0072B2", "TRUE" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Seconds tracked", y = "Share in the center (log scale)") +
  Plot_theme + legend_none()
pA + pB + plot_layout(widths = c(1.2, 1))
```

I drew every session as a point, as in the rest of the book, and I marked the lost ones with a different shape *and* a different color so that the contrast survives a grayscale print (@fig-mdme_of_lost). A table of mean share by group, kept and lost, would give you six numbers and hide that the lost sessions are few and that their shares are all low.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
On the left, compare the open triangles with the filled circles *within the same group*. If the lost sessions were a random sample of the sessions of their group, the triangles would be scattered among the circles; if they sit apart, the loss is related to the outcome. On the right, look at whether the triangles (under 270 seconds) lie in a different part of the cloud from the circles. The mistake to avoid is to conclude "the data are missing at random" because the groups look similar: the comparison that matters is *within* a group.
:::

The lost sessions sit low. Among the ischemic animals of day 1 the mean center share of the kept sessions is `r round(100 * mean(d1$share[d1$surgery == "ischemia" & !d1$short]), 1)`%, and that of the lost ones is `r round(100 * mean(d1$share[d1$surgery == "ischemia" & d1$short]), 1)`% (`r sum(d1$surgery == "ischemia" & d1$short)` sessions). Eight sessions is a small number and the comparison is crude, but it points in one direction, and the direction matters: a rule that removes the sessions with a *low* center share, from the day on which the ischemic animals have a *high* one, inflates the day-1 jump. That is not a missing-at-random loss. What the data cannot say is why: whether the tracker loses a mouse that presses against a wall (where it is not in the center, and is hard to follow), or one that moves little, or something unrelated. I asked, and the answer is that nobody is sure. So I treat the mechanism as unknown, and I do two things: a model that uses the sessions that were only partly seen, and a sensitivity analysis for the part that was not seen.

#### Mice that stop coming {#sec-mdme-dropout}

There is a second kind of absence in the open-field file, and it is the one that I find more worrying. Some animals have no session after day 1, or after day 15: `r sum(tapply(of4$dpi, of4$animal, max) < 22)` of the `r n_of_an` animals. The reason, as far as I know, is that mice die after the surgery, which means that these are not sessions the tracker lost but animals that the experiment lost. The question that makes it a statistical problem is whether the mice that leave are a random sample of the mice, and @tbl-mdme_dropout shows what I can check: where they were on day 1, the last session that they did, among the ischemic animals.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_dropout
#| tbl-cap: "Animals with no session on day 22 (the last day), their last session in the file and their share of tracked time in the center on day 1, with the rank of that share among the ischemic animals of day 1 (1 is the highest of the 37)."

# Last session of every animal, and where its day-1 share sits among the ischemic animals
last_day <- tapply(of4$dpi, of4$animal, max)
leavers <- names(last_day)[last_day < 22]
isch1 <- d1[d1$surgery == "ischemia", ]
isch1$rank <- rank(-isch1$share, ties.method = "min")
drop_tab <- merge(data.frame(animal = leavers, last = as.integer(last_day[leavers])),
                  isch1[, c("animal", "group", "share", "rank")], by = "animal", all.x = TRUE)
drop_tab$share <- round(drop_tab$share, 3)
names(drop_tab) <- c("Animal", "Last session (day)", "Group", "Day-1 center share", "Rank among 37 ischemic animals")
knitr::kable(drop_tab[order(drop_tab$`Last session (day)`), ], row.names = FALSE)
```

The animals that leave after day 1 have day-1 shares at ranks `r paste(sort(drop_tab$"Rank among 37 ischemic animals"[drop_tab$"Last session (day)" == 1]), collapse = ", ")` of `r nrow(isch1)`, all in the top third. Three animals prove nothing, and I will not make a story of them. But the pattern points to a mechanism that I can name: the mice that leave are among those that spent the most time in the center on day 1, a behavior that, in this experiment, goes with a more severe injury. If that is so, the mice that remain are *less affected than the ones that started*, and any statement about the later days that is based only on the mice that remain describes survivors. Here is the part that I find useful: this kind of loss is **missing at random** for a model that contains the day-1 value of each animal, because the loss depends on a number that the model has seen. A model with a level for each animal (@sec-longitudinal-timeseries) uses every session that exists and is valid for the mean under that assumption, while a complete-case analysis that keeps only the animals that have all six sessions is not [@gelman2020; @harrell2015]. The assumption is not testable (maybe the mice died of something the model does not know), but this one is at least a *reasonable* one, and an analysis that makes it explicit is better than one that makes it silently.

#### A sensitivity analysis for what nobody can see {#sec-mdme-tipping}

For the sessions that the tracker lost I cannot assume anything I can check, so I do the other thing the books recommend: I make the assumption a number and move the number. This is a [tipping-point analysis]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}, a form of delta adjustment [@gelman2020; @harrell2015]: assume that the lost sessions differ from the kept ones by an amount $\delta$ on the log-odds scale of the center share, recompute the conclusion for each $\delta$, and look for the $\delta$ at which the conclusion changes (tips). It is the analogue of asking a reviewer "how wrong would my assumption have to be for you to stop believing this?", and the answer is the thing to report.

The conclusion that I test is the jump of day 1: the difference in the mean share of time in the center between ischemic and sham animals, averaged over the two genotypes. I fit it on the kept sessions of day 1 with a zero-inflated beta likelihood, as in the earlier chapters, and a precision for each group, because the sham animals are far less variable than the ischemic ones. Then I add the lost sessions *back by assumption*. If a share $\pi_g$ of the day-1 sessions of group $g$ is lost, and the lost ones have a mean center share $\mu_g^{lost}$ whose log-odds differ from the kept ones by $\delta$, the mean of the whole group is a weighted average (@eq-mdme-delta). With $\delta = 0$ the lost sessions are like the kept ones (missing at random within the group); a negative $\delta$ says that the tracker lost mice that spent less time in the center.

$$
\mu_g(\delta) = (1 - \pi_g)\,\mu_g^{kept} + \pi_g\,\text{logit}^{-1}\!\left(\text{logit}(\mu_g^{kept}) + \delta\right)
$$ {#eq-mdme-delta}

```{r}
#| label: fit-openfield

# Priors on the logit mean of each group and on the log precision of each group
prior_of <- c(prior(normal(-2.5, 1.5), class = "b"), prior(normal(1.5, 1), class = "b", dpar = "phi"))

# 11. Day 1, sessions that meet the 270 s rule (the inherited analysis)
fit_o1 <- brm(
  bf(share ~ 0 + group, phi ~ 0 + group, zi ~ 1),
  data = d1[!d1$short, ], family = zero_inflated_beta(), prior = prior_of,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit11.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 12. Day 1, every session with some tracked time (the lost ones enter with what was seen of them)
fit_o2 <- brm(
  bf(share ~ 0 + group, phi ~ 0 + group, zi ~ 1),
  data = d1, family = zero_inflated_beta(), prior = prior_of,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit12.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
# Group means on the logit scale, group precisions on the log scale, and the zero-inflation probability
summary(fit_o1)
```

### glmmTMB

```{r}
# The same model by maximum likelihood (a precision for each group; no varying terms: one session per animal)
tmb_o1 <- glmmTMB(share ~ 0 + group, dispformula = ~ 0 + group, ziformula = ~ 1,
                  family = beta_family(), data = d1[!d1$short, ])
summary(tmb_o1)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: tipping

# Posterior of the four group means (the zero-inflated mean) on the kept sessions, and on all sessions
nd_g <- data.frame(group = factor(levels(d1$group), levels = levels(d1$group)))
m_kept <- posterior_epred(fit_o1, newdata = nd_g)
m_all <- posterior_epred(fit_o2, newdata = nd_g)

# Share of the day-1 sessions that were lost, by group
pi_lost <- as.numeric(tapply(d1$short, d1$group, mean))

# The group means after adding the lost sessions with a shift delta on the logit scale (equation above)
adj_means <- function(m, delta) {
  out <- m
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(m))) out[, j] <- (1 - pi_lost[j]) * m[, j] + pi_lost[j] * plogis(qlogis(m[, j]) + delta)
  out
}

# The conclusion: mean share of ischemic animals minus that of shams (percentage points), over genotypes
jump_fun <- function(m) 100 * (rowMeans(m[, c(2, 4)]) - rowMeans(m[, c(1, 3)]))

# A grid of deltas; -Inf is the extreme in which every lost session had no time in the center at all
delta_grid <- c(-Inf, seq(-6, 3, by = 0.5))
tip_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(delta_grid, function(d) {
  q <- quantile(jump_fun(adj_means(m_kept, d)), c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975, 0.25, 0.75))
  data.frame(delta = d, med = q[1], lo = q[2], hi = q[3], lo50 = q[4], hi50 = q[5])
}))

# What the partly tracked sessions themselves suggest: the log-odds difference between lost and kept
# sessions among the ischemic animals
isch_d1 <- d1[d1$surgery == "ischemia", ]
delta_obs <- qlogis(mean(isch_d1$share[isch_d1$short])) - qlogis(mean(isch_d1$share[!isch_d1$short]))

# The jump with no adjustment, with the lost sessions added as seen (all sessions), and at the extreme
jump_kept <- jump_fun(m_kept)
jump_all <- jump_fun(m_all)
jump_extreme <- jump_fun(adj_means(m_kept, -Inf))
jump_obs <- jump_fun(adj_means(m_kept, delta_obs))
```

@fig-mdme_tipping shows the result. On the kept sessions, the ischemic animals spend `r qs(jump_kept, 1)` percentage points more of the tracked time in the center on day 1 than the shams do. If I add the lost sessions with the shift that the partly tracked sessions themselves suggest ($\delta =$ `r round(delta_obs, 1)`) the jump is `r qs(jump_obs, 1)`; if every lost session had no time in the center at all, the most extreme case that I can imagine, it is `r qs(jump_extreme, 1)`. And the model that simply uses the lost sessions with what was seen of them, no assumption about the unseen seconds, gives `r qs(jump_all, 1)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_tipping
#| fig-cap: "Tipping-point analysis of the day-1 jump in the center share (ischemic minus sham, percentage points). The horizontal axis is delta, the shift on the logit scale that the lost sessions are assumed to have relative to the kept ones; delta = 0 means the lost sessions are like the kept ones. The line is the posterior median and the bands the 50% and 95% intervals. The leftmost value stands for a delta of minus infinity: every lost session with no time in the center. The dotted vertical lines mark delta = 0 and the shift suggested by the partly tracked sessions; the horizontal dashed line marks no difference."
#| fig-alt: "A line on a plane with delta on the horizontal axis from minus infinity to 3 and the jump in percentage points on the vertical axis from 0 to 30. The line is flat at about 11 percentage points from minus infinity to about minus 3, rises to about 14.5 at delta zero and to about 20 at delta 2. Two shaded bands around it (50% and 95%) stay above the dashed horizontal line at zero everywhere; the lower limit of the 95% band is about 4.5. Two dotted vertical lines mark delta equal to zero and delta equal to minus 1.6."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| warning: false

# Place the minus-infinity case at the left edge of the axis, and mark the two reference values
tip_plot <- tip_df
tip_plot$x <- ifelse(is.infinite(tip_plot$delta), -8, tip_plot$delta)
ggplot(tip_plot, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo50, ymax = hi50), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = med), color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, delta_obs), linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.1, y = 29, label = "lost = kept", hjust = 0, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = delta_obs - 0.1, y = 29, label = "as the partial\nsessions suggest", hjust = 1, size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-8, -6, -4, -2, 0, 2), labels = c("-Inf", "-6", "-4", "-2", "0", "2")) +
  labs(x = "Delta: shift in the log-odds of the lost sessions",
       y = "Jump on day 1 (percentage points)") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
The horizontal axis is an assumption, not a measurement: how different the sessions that the tracker lost were from the ones it kept, with 0 meaning "not different" and negative values meaning "they spent less time in the center". The vertical axis is the conclusion. Read the line from the 0 to the left, which is the direction that the data suggest, and ask whether the band ever touches the dashed line at zero. If it does, the position of that crossing is the *tipping point*, and the question to ask is whether such an assumption is plausible. If the band never touches it, the conclusion does not depend on the assumption, within the range that you drew. The mistake to avoid is to read the figure as saying that the assumption is true: it says how much it would have to be false for the answer to change.
:::

The conclusion about the jump does not tip. The lower limit of the interval stays above zero across the whole range, down to the extreme case in which every lost session had no time in the center, and the reason is arithmetic that you can check by hand (@eq-mdme-delta): only `r round(100 * mean(pi_lost[c(2, 4)]), 0)`% of the ischemic sessions of day 1 were lost, so even if every one of them had a center share of zero, the mean of the ischemic groups could fall by at most that share of what it was. What *does* change is the size of the jump, from `r round(median(jump_kept), 1)` percentage points to `r round(median(jump_extreme), 1)` at the extreme, which says that the inherited rule makes the jump look larger than it is, in the direction that @fig-mdme_of_lost suggested, but not by enough to reverse it. That is the form that a result about missing data should take: not "the data are missing at random", which I cannot know, but "the conclusion holds for every shift I can think of, and the size depends on it as follows".

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`glmmTMB` (@brooks2017) fits the same zero-inflated beta by maximum likelihood, and the group means that it reports agree with the posterior medians of `brms`, as they should with a day-1 sample of 38 animals and weak priors. What the frequentist fit cannot do is the next step: a tipping-point analysis is a calculation on the *estimated* means, so I can run it on the maximum-likelihood estimates as well, but there is no distribution of the jump to carry the uncertainty through unless I resample (bootstrap) the animals. The Bayesian fit gives that distribution for free, which is the practical reason why the book keeps `brms` first in a sensitivity analysis. A frequentist counterpart of the *reasoning* is a pattern-mixture model fitted by hand, which is the equation above; the textbooks present it as the standard way to examine data that are missing not at random [@harrell2015].
:::

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results.** On day 1, ischemic mice spent `r qs(jump_kept, 1)` percentage points more of the tracked time in the center of the open field than sham-operated mice (posterior median and 95% credible interval, sessions with at least 270 s tracked). `r sum(d1$short)` of the `r nrow(d1)` day-1 sessions had less than 270 s tracked and were excluded; their share of time in the center, in the part that was seen, was lower than that of the retained sessions. In a tipping-point analysis, the 95% interval of the difference excluded zero for every shift in the log-odds of the center share of the excluded sessions between minus infinity (no time in the center) and `r max(delta_grid)`; the difference was `r qs(jump_obs, 1)` percentage points with the shift suggested by the partially tracked sessions (`r round(delta_obs, 1)`) and `r qs(jump_extreme, 1)` in the extreme case.

**Methods.** The share of the tracked time in the center was modeled with a zero-inflated beta likelihood, with a mean and a precision for each of four groups (genotype by surgery) in `brms` (four chains of 2,000 iterations; R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above 400 for all parameters). Excluded sessions were added to the group means by assumption, with a shift $\delta$ on the logit scale (pattern-mixture; equation above). Loss of sessions after day 1 (`r length(leavers)` animals, attributed to postoperative mortality) was not modeled.
:::

### The NeuN sections {#sec-mdme-neun-sections}

The other absent values of this part are the brain sections of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts. I told you then that sections go missing when the tissue is damaged or badly cut, that this can be related to the injury, and that I would come back. The question I asked Daniel was *why* some mice have fewer sections, and the answer is that sections are lost when the brain is in poor condition, which may be related to specific days after ischemia in which the tissue is more fragile. That is a mechanism, and it makes a prediction: the missing sections should concentrate in ischemic mice, on the fragile days. @fig-mdme_sections tests it on the file.

```{r}
#| label: prep-neun
#| include: false

# The NeuN file of the first multilevel chapter, rebuilt from the raw data (all structures)
neun_raw <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/5x_NeuN_AnnotationsSummary.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
area_col <- grep("^Area", names(neun_raw), value = TRUE)
neun <- data.frame(image = neun_raw$Image, structure = neun_raw$Name, class = neun_raw$Class,
                   detections = neun_raw[["Num Detections"]], positive = neun_raw[["Num Positive"]],
                   area_um2 = neun_raw[[area_col]])
parts <- strsplit(sub("\\.tif$", "", neun$image), "_")
neun$mouse <- sapply(parts, `[`, 3)
neun$dpi_days <- as.integer(sub("D$", "", sapply(parts, `[`, 4)))
neun$scene_n <- as.integer(sub("Scene", "", sapply(parts, `[`, 5)))
neun$hemi <- factor(sub(":.*$", "", neun$class), levels = c("Right", "Left"))
neun$section <- paste(neun$mouse, neun$scene_n, sep = ":")
neun$dpi <- factor(paste0(neun$dpi_days, "D"), levels = c("0D", "5D", "15D", "30D"))
neun$area_mm2 <- neun$area_um2 / 1e6
neun$structure <- factor(neun$structure, levels = c("CTX", "CNU", "IB", "MB", "fiber tracts"))
neun$mouse <- factor(neun$mouse)
neun$section <- factor(neun$section)
stopifnot(nrow(neun) == 1484, nlevels(neun$mouse) == 31)

# Cortex, as in the earlier chapters, with the log of the density
cortex <- neun[neun$structure == "CTX", ]
cortex$log_dens <- log(cortex$positive / cortex$area_mm2)

# For each mouse and each of the seven scenes: was the section measured, and if not, did the series
# end there (no later section exists) or was it lost inside the series?
mice_df <- unique(neun[, c("mouse", "dpi")])
sec_grid <- expand.grid(mouse = mice_df$mouse, scene_n = 1:7)
sec_grid$dpi <- mice_df$dpi[match(sec_grid$mouse, mice_df$mouse)]
have <- paste(neun$mouse, neun$scene_n)
sec_grid$present <- paste(sec_grid$mouse, sec_grid$scene_n) %in% have
last_scene <- tapply(neun$scene_n, neun$mouse, max)
sec_grid$status <- ifelse(sec_grid$present, "Measured",
```
