```{r}
                          ifelse(sec_grid$scene_n > last_scene[as.character(sec_grid$mouse)],
                                 "Series ends before it", "Lost inside the series"))
sec_grid$status <- factor(sec_grid$status, levels = c("Measured", "Series ends before it", "Lost inside the series"))
n_lost_in <- sum(sec_grid$status == "Lost inside the series")
mice_lost <- as.character(unique(sec_grid$mouse[sec_grid$status == "Lost inside the series"]))
n_end <- sum(sec_grid$status == "Series ends before it")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_sections
#| fig-cap: "The sections of the NeuN experiment: one row per mouse and one column per section (1 anterior, 7 posterior), by day after ischemia. Filled circles: the section is in the file. Open circles: the section is not in the file because the series of that mouse ends earlier. Crosses: the section is missing inside the series (a gap between sections that exist)."
#| fig-alt: "A grid with 31 mouse rows grouped into four panels (0, 5, 15 and 30 days) and seven columns. Nearly every cell is a filled circle. Open circles appear in column 7 for 15 mice, in all four panels, including four of the five mice of day 0. Four crosses appear inside the series, in three mice from days 5 and 15: one in column 6, two in columns 4 and 5, and one in column 5."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 8
#| warning: false

# One mark per mouse and section; shape and color agree so that the figure survives grayscale
sg <- sec_grid[order(sec_grid$dpi, sec_grid$mouse), ]
sg$mouse <- factor(sg$mouse, levels = rev(unique(sg$mouse)))
n_by_d <- table(mice_df$dpi)
sg$panel <- factor(paste0(sg$dpi, " (", n_by_d[as.character(sg$dpi)], " mice)"),
                   levels = paste0(names(n_by_d), " (", n_by_d, " mice)"))
ggplot(sg, aes(x = scene_n, y = mouse, shape = status, color = status)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, stroke = 1) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Measured" = 16, "Series ends before it" = 1, "Lost inside the series" = 4)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Measured" = "black", "Series ends before it" = "grey55", "Lost inside the series" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Section (1 = anterior, 7 = posterior)", y = "Mouse", shape = NULL, color = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8), strip.text = element_text(size = 10)) +
  legend_top()
```

I took the figure of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts and made one change, which is the point of this section: a missing section is not one thing. `r n_end` sections are missing at the *end* of the series, section 7 of mice whose last section is the sixth (@fig-mdme_sections, open circles). They are found in all four panels, including four of the five mice of day 0, which had no ischemia, so whatever makes the series stop at six sections is not the injury. It looks like a matter of how far back the series was cut. Only `r n_lost_in` sections are missing *inside* a series, in `r length(mice_lost)` mice (`r paste(mice_lost, collapse = ", ")`), and these are the ones that fit the story of damaged tissue: all of them are from ischemic days (5 and 15), and one of them (M16) also has a region in section 6 with a large area and no detected cell at all, which looks more like a failure of the detection than like an empty region. I report that as what it is: `r length(mice_lost)` mice out of 31 with a plausible loss related to the tissue, and a larger and probably harmless loss of the last section.

Regions inside a section can also be absent, and these are not accidents of cutting but of anatomy. The cerebral nuclei (CNU) are not in the most posterior section, the interbrain (IB) is not in the first one and barely in the second, and the midbrain (MB) appears only from the fifth section on (@fig-mdme_structures). That is a [structural zero]{.ix ix="structural zero"}: a region that cannot be there, and that is not a measurement of "no cells". Entering it as a zero count would be a mistake of the same family as the `Td79` total that I describe below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_structures
#| fig-cap: "Share of sections in which each structure was annotated, by section number (1 anterior, 7 posterior). The number in each tile is how many sections had the structure. Empty tiles are structurally absent: the structure is not in that part of the brain."
#| fig-alt: "A tile map with five structures on the vertical axis (cortex, cerebral nuclei, interbrain, midbrain, fiber tracts) and seven sections on the horizontal axis. Cortex and fiber tracts are present in nearly every section, from 31 in section 1 to 16 in section 7. Cerebral nuclei are present in 21 of 31 sections in section 1, in sections 2 to 6, and in none of section 7. Interbrain is absent from section 1, present in 6 sections of section 2 and in nearly all from section 3. Midbrain is absent from sections 1 to 4, present in one section of section 5, in 21 of 30 of section 6 and in all 16 of section 7."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| warning: false

# How many sections have each structure, out of the sections that exist for that scene number
sec_unique <- unique(neun[, c("section", "scene_n")])
n_sec_scene <- table(sec_unique$scene_n)
st_tab <- as.data.frame(table(unique(neun[, c("section", "scene_n", "structure")])[, c("scene_n", "structure")]))
names(st_tab) <- c("scene_n", "structure", "n")
st_tab$total <- as.integer(n_sec_scene[as.character(st_tab$scene_n)])
st_tab$share <- st_tab$n / st_tab$total
st_tab$scene_n <- as.integer(as.character(st_tab$scene_n))
st_tab$structure <- factor(st_tab$structure, levels = rev(levels(neun$structure)))

# Tile map: the fill is the share of sections, the label the number of sections
ggplot(st_tab, aes(x = scene_n, y = structure, fill = share)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(n == 0, "", n)), size = 3.6, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#56B4E9", limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_percent(),
                      name = "Share of sections") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(x = "Section (1 = anterior, 7 = posterior)", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme + legend_right() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12))
```

Last, a different thing again: the five rows of the file with no positive cell. They are shown in @tbl-mdme_zero_rows, and they are three different things that happen to share a zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_zero_rows
#| tbl-cap: "The five annotated regions with no NeuN-positive cell, with their detections, area and what I think each one is."

# The zero rows, their size, and my reading of each
zr <- neun[neun$positive == 0, c("mouse", "dpi", "scene_n", "hemi", "structure", "detections", "positive", "area_mm2")]
zr$area_mm2 <- round(zr$area_mm2, 3)
zr$reading <- ifelse(zr$detections > 0, "A sliver with only negative cells",
              ifelse(zr$area_mm2 > 1, "No cell of any kind in a large region: probably a failed detection, not an empty region",
                     "A sliver of the structure at the edge of the section: too small to contain a cell"))
names(zr) <- c("Mouse", "DPI", "Section", "Hemisphere", "Structure", "Detections", "Positive", "Area (mm2)", "Reading")
knitr::kable(zr, row.names = FALSE)
```

None of the five is a count of zero that means "this region has no neurons". Two are slivers of the midbrain at the edge of a section, with an area of about a thousandth of a square millimeter, where a count of zero is what an area that small should give; one is a sliver of the cerebral nuclei with some negative cells and no positive ones; and two, the left and right cerebral nuclei of the same section of mouse M16, have a large area and not a single detection, which is where I would go and look at the images. The habit is the one of @sec-eda-data-quality: a zero is a claim, and it has to be checked before it enters a model.

What should be done with the sections that are missing? The honest answer is that the multilevel model of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts already does most of it. It uses every section that exists, it does not need the same number from each mouse, and a mouse with fewer sections is a mouse about which we know a little less. What I can add is a sensitivity analysis for the one comparison that matters, the ratio of the density of NeuN-positive cells in the left (injured) cortex to that of the right, by day after ischemia: fit it on all sections, fit it on the sections that all mice share (the first six), and fit it without the `r length(mice_lost)` mice that lost sections inside the series.

```{r}
#| label: fit-neun-sections

# Priors on the log density (cells per mm2): intercept around 850 cells, coefficients and spreads as before
prior_neun <- c(prior(normal(6.7, 0.5), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
                prior(exponential(3), class = "sd"), prior(exponential(3), class = "sigma"))
f_neun <- log_dens ~ hemi * dpi + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section)

# 13. All sections
fit_s1 <- brm(f_neun, data = cortex, prior = prior_neun, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123,
              iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit13.rds", file_refit = "never")

# 14. Only sections 1 to 6, which every mouse has
fit_s2 <- brm(f_neun, data = cortex[cortex$scene_n <= 6, ], prior = prior_neun, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123,
              iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit14.rds", file_refit = "never")

# 15. Without the mice that lost sections inside the series
fit_s3 <- brm(f_neun, data = cortex[!(cortex$mouse %in% mice_lost), ], prior = prior_neun, chains = 4, cores = 4,
              seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit15.rds", file_refit = "never")
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
# Population effects and spreads of the model on all sections
summary(fit_s1)
```

### lme4

```{r}
# The same model by restricted maximum likelihood
lmer_s1 <- lmer(log_dens ~ hemi * dpi + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section), data = cortex)
summary(lmer_s1)
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_neun_sens
#| fig-cap: "Ratio of the density of NeuN-positive cells in the left cortex to that in the right cortex, by day after ischemia, under three ways of handling the missing sections. Points are posterior medians and bars 95% credible intervals. A ratio of 1 (dotted line) means no difference between hemispheres."
#| fig-alt: "Four rows (0, 5, 15 and 30 days after ischemia) and, in each, three points with horizontal intervals on a logarithmic axis from about 0.5 to 1.3. At day 0 the ratio is about 1.1. At 5 days it is about 0.75, at 15 days about 0.65 and at 30 days about 0.8. The three analyses (all sections, sections 1 to 6, without the two mice with lost sections) give almost the same point and interval in every row."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

# Left to right log-ratio at each day: the hemisphere coefficient plus the interaction of that day
lr_draws <- function(fit) {
  d <- as_draws_df(fit)
  data.frame(`0D` = d$b_hemiLeft, `5D` = d$b_hemiLeft + d$`b_hemiLeft:dpi5D`,
             `15D` = d$b_hemiLeft + d$`b_hemiLeft:dpi15D`, `30D` = d$b_hemiLeft + d$`b_hemiLeft:dpi30D`,
             check.names = FALSE)
}
lr_all <- lr_draws(fit_s1); lr_six <- lr_draws(fit_s2); lr_out <- lr_draws(fit_s3)
sens_neun <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lr_all), function(dd) rbind(
  qrow(exp(lr_all[[dd]]), "All sections", dd),
  qrow(exp(lr_six[[dd]]), "Sections 1 to 6 only", dd),
  qrow(exp(lr_out[[dd]]), "Without mice with lost sections", dd))))
sens_neun$group <- factor(sens_neun$group, levels = rev(names(lr_all)))
sens_neun$label <- factor(sens_neun$label, levels = c("All sections", "Sections 1 to 6 only", "Without mice with lost sections"))

# Three analyses per day, dodged vertically
ggplot(sens_neun, aes(x = med, y = group, xmin = lo, xmax = hi, color = label, shape = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.5, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.3)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("All sections" = "#000000", "Sections 1 to 6 only" = "#E69F00", "Without mice with lost sections" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 15, 17)) +
  labs(x = "Left to right density ratio (log scale)", y = "Days after ischemia", color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme + legend_top() + guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

@fig-mdme_neun_sens reads like the earlier forest: look at the *position* of the three points in each row, not at whether the interval touches 1. In every row the three analyses agree to within a small fraction of the width of their intervals, so the conclusion of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts about how much the injured cortex loses does not depend on whether the missing sections are in or out. At 15 days the ratio is `r qs(exp(lr_all[["15D"]]), 2)` with all the sections, `r qs(exp(lr_six[["15D"]]), 2)` with sections 1 to 6 and `r qs(exp(lr_out[["15D"]]), 2)` without the `r length(mice_lost)` mice. That is the result that I can honestly give: the loss of sections is not a threat to this comparison, as far as I can examine it, and what I cannot examine (that the sections lost inside the series were the most damaged ones, so the density would have been lower still) would make the loss *larger*, not smaller. The direction of the bias is known, and it works against the effect that we report.

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`lme4` fits the same two varying intercepts by restricted maximum likelihood and gives the same fixed effects to the second decimal, since a Gaussian model with `r nlevels(cortex$mouse)` mice and `r nlevels(cortex$section)` sections has enough data for the likelihood to dominate the weak priors. The model of the sections as a whole has the same property as the open-field model: both treat the sections that exist as informative about the ones that do not, which is the missing-at-random assumption written in a likelihood. If it were wrong, neither would warn you.
:::

## Blurred: a count has an error bar that the spreadsheet does not show {#sec-mdme-blurred}

The third jar is the one that scientists forget to open, because nothing in the file says it is there. A NeuN density is a count of positive cells divided by the area of a region, and a count made by a microscope and a counting rule is a *sample* of the cells in the tissue: if I could cut the same section again and count again, I would not get the same number. The [counting error]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"} of a count is known, to a good approximation, and that is what makes it a clean case of [measurement error]{style="color:green; font-weight:bold;"}: for a Poisson count of $n$ cells the standard deviation is $\sqrt{n}$, so the *relative* error is $1/\sqrt{n}$. A thousand cells give an error of about 3%; a hundred give 10%; ten give 32%. The question is not whether it exists, but *whether it is big enough to matter*, and the way to answer it is to put it next to the spread that you care about.

I do that in @fig-mdme_counting for every structure of the NeuN experiment. For each section I plot the relative counting error of its count (`1 / sqrt(count)`) and next to it, as a black bar, the standard deviation of the log density between sections of the same day and hemisphere, which is the biological and technical variation that the model of @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts is about. Both are on the same scale (a proportion of the density), so a point below the bar is a count whose error is smaller than the spread between sections.

```{r}
#| label: prep-error
#| include: false

# Sections with at least one positive cell: log density, counting error of the log density (1 / sqrt(count))
nz <- neun[neun$positive > 0, ]
nz$log_dens <- log(nz$positive / nz$area_mm2)
nz$sei <- 1 / sqrt(nz$positive)
n_zero_rows <- sum(neun$positive == 0)

# Spread of the log density between sections, after removing the mean of each day and hemisphere
spread_by <- sapply(levels(nz$structure), function(s) {
  z <- nz[nz$structure == s, ]
  sd(resid(lm(log_dens ~ interaction(dpi, hemi), data = z)))
})
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_counting
#| fig-cap: "Relative counting error of the NeuN count of every section (points; 1 divided by the square root of the count, logarithmic axis) by structure, against the spread of the log density between sections of the same day and hemisphere (black bars). The error of a count is small everywhere, and smallest in the cortex, where counts are in the thousands."
#| fig-alt: "Five columns (cortex, cerebral nuclei, interbrain, midbrain, fiber tracts) and a logarithmic vertical axis from 0.5 to 100 percent. In each column, a cloud of grey points sits between about 0.7 and 25 percent, with a median near 1 percent for cortex and about 3.5 percent for fiber tracts. A black horizontal bar in each column sits much higher, between about 30 and 65 percent. A few points in the cerebral nuclei and fiber tracts rise above 10 percent, and one reaches about 25 percent."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| warning: false

# Counting error of every section as a point, and the spread between sections as a bar
bar_df <- data.frame(structure = factor(names(spread_by), levels = levels(nz$structure)), spread = as.numeric(spread_by))
set.seed(3)
ggplot(nz, aes(x = structure, y = sei)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, size = 0.9, alpha = 0.35, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_errorbar(data = bar_df, aes(y = spread, ymin = spread, ymax = spread), width = 0.6, linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x, 1), "%"), breaks = c(0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Relative counting error (points)\nand spread between sections (bars)") +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12))
```

The picture is drawn with `ggplot2::geom_jitter()` so that every one of the `r nrow(nz)` regions (a structure in one hemisphere of one section) is visible, because the interesting thing is the *tail*: the median section has a tiny error, and a few have a large one. A table of mean errors per structure would give you the first and hide the second.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read this figure"}
Read it in two steps. First compare each cloud of points with the bar in its own column: if the cloud is far below the bar, the counting error is small next to the variation between sections and a model that treats the count as exact loses almost nothing. Second look for the points that climb toward the bar: those are the sections with few cells, the ones where the count is the weakest evidence. The mistake to avoid is to read a small counting error as a statement that the *density* is precise: it says that the count is a good sample of the tissue that was counted, and nothing about whether the section is typical of the animal.
:::

The result is a finding, not a failure: **in this experiment the counting error is small next to the biology.** In the cortex the median relative error is `r round(100 * median(nz$sei[nz$structure == "CTX"]), 1)`% against a spread between sections of `r round(100 * spread_by[["CTX"]])`%, and even in the structures with the smallest counts, the fiber tracts, the median error is `r round(100 * median(nz$sei[nz$structure == "fiber tracts"]), 1)`% against a spread of `r round(100 * spread_by[["fiber tracts"]])`%. In variance terms, which is what a model sees, the counting error accounts for about `r round(100 * mean(nz$sei[nz$structure == "CTX"]^2) / spread_by[["CTX"]]^2, 1)`% of the variance of the cortex and `r round(100 * mean(nz$sei[nz$structure == "fiber tracts"]^2) / spread_by[["fiber tracts"]]^2, 1)`% of that of the fiber tracts. A rule that I find useful is to compare the average of $1/n$ with the variance of the log density you are modeling: when the first is below a few percent of the second, the error does not matter for the mean. The books agree on the principle: the rate is a latent quantity, and treating a ratio of counts as if it were known matters when counts are small or when the exposure (here, the area) varies a lot between units, and it can be ignored when the biological variation is much larger than the counting noise [@mcelreath2020].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_error_share
#| tbl-cap: "Counting error against the spread between sections, by structure: number of sections, median count, median relative error, spread of the log density (standard deviation), share of its variance that the counting error accounts for, and number of sections with fewer than 100 cells."

# One row per structure
err_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(nz$structure), function(s) {
  z <- nz[nz$structure == s, ]
  data.frame(Structure = s, Sections = nrow(z), `Median count` = round(median(z$positive)),
             `Median error (%)` = round(100 * median(z$sei), 1),
             `Spread (SD of log density)` = round(spread_by[[s]], 2),
             `Variance due to counting (%)` = round(100 * mean(z$sei^2) / spread_by[[s]]^2, 1),
             `Sections under 100 cells` = sum(z$positive < 100), check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(err_tab)
```

Where does the counting error matter, then? Where there are few cells. The fiber tracts, the cerebral nuclei, the interbrain and the midbrain have `r sum(nz$positive < 100 & nz$structure != "CTX")` regions with fewer than 100 positive cells (@tbl-mdme_error_share), with relative errors of 10% or more, and the smallest regions are slivers at the edge of a section. In those, a model that treats the density as exact gives a count of 20 the same weight as a count of 2,000, which is the problem that the books name: a ratio of counts is a rate with a precision that depends on the denominator [@mcelreath2020]. There are two ways to give the model what it needs, and I show both on the fiber tracts, which are the structure with the most small counts.

The first is to keep the log density as the outcome and tell the model *how precisely each one is known*. In `brms` the term `se(sei, sigma = TRUE)` on the left of the formula says that each observation has a known standard error `sei`, here $1/\sqrt{n}$, on the log scale, and that there is, in addition, a residual spread `sigma` to be estimated (the variation between sections that is *not* the counting error). The second is to model the counts themselves, with the log of the area as an offset and a negative binomial likelihood, which is what @sec-count-regression and @sec-multilevel-glmm did: a count model carries the Poisson error automatically, because the variance of a count is part of its distribution, and a region with zero cells stays in (there are five in the cerebral nuclei and the midbrain, none in the fiber tracts), which the log density cannot do.

```{r}
#| label: fit-error

# Fiber tracts: the structure with the smallest counts
ft <- nz[nz$structure == "fiber tracts", ]
ft_all <- neun[neun$structure == "fiber tracts", ]
mu0 <- round(median(ft$log_dens), 1)
prior_ft <- c(prior_string(paste0("normal(", mu0, ", 1)"), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
              prior(exponential(3), class = "sd"), prior(exponential(3), class = "sigma"))
prior_ft_nb <- c(prior_string(paste0("normal(", mu0, ", 1)"), class = "Intercept"), prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b"),
                 prior(inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3), class = "shape"), prior(exponential(3), class = "sd"))

# 16. The log density as if it were exact
fit_e1 <- brm(
  log_dens ~ hemi * dpi + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section),
  data = ft, prior = prior_ft, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 6000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit16.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 17. The same, with the known counting error of each section (an extra spread sigma is still estimated)
fit_e2 <- brm(
  log_dens | se(sei, sigma = TRUE) ~ hemi * dpi + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section),
  data = ft, prior = prior_ft, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 6000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit17.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 18. The counts with the log of the area as an offset (the Poisson error is part of the distribution)
fit_e3 <- brm(
  positive ~ hemi * dpi + offset(log(area_mm2)) + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section),
  data = ft_all, family = negbinomial(), prior = prior_ft_nb,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 3000, control = ml_control, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit18.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms: se()

```{r}
# Population effects, spreads and the extra residual scale (sigma) of the model with known counting error
summary(fit_e2)
```

### brms: count model

```{r}
# The count model with the area as an offset
summary(fit_e3)
```

### lme4 and glmmTMB

```{r}
# Frequentist counterparts: the log density without the error term, and the count model with the offset
lmer_e1 <- lmer(log_dens ~ hemi * dpi + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section), data = ft)
tmb_e3 <- glmmTMB(positive ~ hemi * dpi + offset(log(area_mm2)) + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section),
                  family = nbinom2(), data = ft_all)
summary(tmb_e3)
```
:::

The first thing I look at is `sigma`. In the plain model `sigma` is `r qs(as_draws_df(fit_e1)$sigma, 2)` and it absorbs everything between sections, the counting error included. In the model with `se()` the extra spread is `r qs(as_draws_df(fit_e2)$sigma, 2)`: it is smaller, since the part that is the known counting error was subtracted from it, and the difference is the share of the variance that I could attribute to the measurement. It is a small difference, as the figure promised, and the effects of interest should not move. @fig-mdme_se_compare shows the ratio of the density of the left fiber tracts to that of the right, by day, under the three models.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_se_compare
#| fig-cap: "Ratio of the density of NeuN-positive cells in the left fiber tracts to that in the right, by day after ischemia, under three models: the log density as if it were exact, the log density with the known counting error of each section (se), and the counts with an area offset (negative binomial). Points are posterior medians and bars 95% credible intervals."
#| fig-alt: "Four rows (0, 5, 15 and 30 days) with three points each on a logarithmic horizontal axis from about 0.6 to 1.6. The three models give nearly the same point and interval in every row. The ratios are close to 1 at all days, with intervals that cross 1 in most rows."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| warning: false

# Left to right log-ratio by day, for each of the three models
lr3 <- list(`Log density, as if exact` = lr_draws(fit_e1), `Log density with se()` = lr_draws(fit_e2),
            `Counts with area offset` = lr_draws(fit_e3))
se_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lr3), function(m) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(lr3[[m]]), function(dd) qrow(exp(lr3[[m]][[dd]]), m, dd)))))
se_df$group <- factor(se_df$group, levels = rev(c("0D", "5D", "15D", "30D")))
se_df$label <- factor(se_df$label, levels = names(lr3))

# Three models per day, dodged vertically
ggplot(se_df, aes(x = med, y = group, xmin = lo, xmax = hi, color = label, shape = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.5, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#000000", "#E69F00", "#0072B2")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 15, 17)) +
  labs(x = "Left to right density ratio (log scale)", y = "Days after ischemia", color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  Plot_theme + legend_top() + guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3))
```

In @fig-mdme_se_compare the three models agree. At 15 days the ratio is `r qs(exp(lr3[[1]][["15D"]]), 2)` as if exact, `r qs(exp(lr3[[2]][["15D"]]), 2)` with the counting error and `r qs(exp(lr3[[3]][["15D"]]), 2)` with the count model. I did not expect more, and I do not want to pretend that I did: the counting error is `r round(100 * mean(ft$sei^2) / spread_by[["fiber tracts"]]^2, 1)`% of the variance of the fiber tracts, and a model that is correct about 1% of the variance cannot change the answer by much. The measurement-error model is *not* wrong here; it is a more complete description that, in this experiment, does not change the conclusion. It would change it if the counts were much smaller (a region of a few dozen cells in every section), or if the area varied by orders of magnitude between the units being compared (a count of 20 in a sliver is not comparable to a count of 20 in a full region), and the way to know is the comparison of @fig-mdme_counting, which is cheap.

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
`lme4` has no way of declaring a known variance for each observation, so the frequentist version of the `se()` model is not available there. The tool that exists is the meta-analytic one, `metafor::rma.mv()`, which takes the sampling variances of each observation and estimates the rest; it is not installed in this project and I did not run it. What the frequentist route does have is the count model: `glmmTMB` with a negative binomial and an offset fits the same model as the third `brms` fit (above) and gives the same left to right ratios, since the offset carries the denominator and the negative binomial carries the sampling error. That is also the practical advice that I would give: when the outcome is a count over an area, the count model with an offset is the simplest way to take the counting error seriously.
:::

#### The distribution of the measurement error is also a model {#sec-mdme-sigma}

The chapter on distributional regression promised that the variance of the *measurement* would become one more thing to model (@sec-multivariate-distributional-regression), and the `se()` term is where that promise is kept. The known counting error enters as a fixed part of the variance, and the extra spread, the one that is *not* counting error, can have a formula of its own. The biological question is natural: is the injured hemisphere more variable than the intact one, after taking the counting error out?

```{r}
#| label: fit-error-sigma

# 19. The extra spread (not the counting error) is allowed to differ between hemispheres
fit_e4 <- brm(
  bf(log_dens | se(sei, sigma = TRUE) ~ hemi * dpi + (1 | mouse) + (1 | section), sigma ~ hemi),
  data = ft, prior = c(prior_ft[prior_ft$class != "sigma", ], prior(normal(-1, 1), class = "Intercept", dpar = "sigma"),
                       prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b", dpar = "sigma")),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 6000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit19.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
dr_e4 <- as_draws_df(fit_e4)
sd_ratio <- exp(dr_e4$b_sigma_hemiLeft)
```

The extra spread of the left fiber tracts is `r qs(sd_ratio, 2)` times that of the right (posterior median and 95% credible interval), with a posterior probability of `r round(mean(sd_ratio > 1), 2)` that it is larger. I would not build anything on that number, but the *form* of the model is what I want you to keep: a known measurement variance that is subtracted by the model, plus a spread that is estimated and can be modeled, which is the decomposition that a reader of a methods section wants and almost never gets.

### An error in a predictor is a different problem {#sec-mdme-me}

What I have described is measurement error in an *outcome*, and the books are clear that it is the benign case: noise in $y$ folds into the residual, it widens the intervals and it does not bias the slope [@gelman2020; @mcelreath2020]. Noise in a *predictor* is not benign, because it pulls the slope toward zero (attenuation): if you regress a response on a noisy version of $x$, a part of the variation of $x_{obs}$ is noise that has nothing to do with the response, and the slope is diluted by the share of the variance of $x_{obs}$ that is true signal (the *reliability*). In `brms` the term is `me(x, sdx)`, which declares a latent true $x$ with the observed one distributed around it with the known standard deviation `sdx`.

I have a real case in the data that I already know, and I run it in order to see what happens, not to find an effect. In `cell_data` the number of PDGFR-β+ cells (`Pdgfrb_Pos`) is a count, with a Poisson counting error, and the question can be: *at the same day, do animals with more PDGFR-β+ cells have a higher GFAP integrated density?* The predictor is the count (on the log scale, with an error of $1/\sqrt{n}$) and the outcome is the log of the GFAP integrated density.

```{r}
#| label: fit-me

# The histology table: one row per animal (49 animals); log of the PDGFR-beta+ count and its counting error
cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data$DPI_f <- factor(cell_data$DPI)
cell_data$log_gfap <- log(cell_data$Gfap_IntDen)
cell_data$log_pos <- log(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos)
cell_data$sd_log_pos <- 1 / sqrt(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos)

# Reliability of the log count at the same day: share of its variance that is not counting error
res_lp <- resid(lm(log_pos ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data))
reliab <- 1 - mean(cell_data$sd_log_pos^2) / var(res_lp)

# 20. The slope of log GFAP on the log count, as if the count were exact
fit_x1 <- brm(
  log_gfap ~ DPI_f + log_pos,
  data = cell_data, prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b"), prior(normal(6, 3), class = "Intercept"),
                              prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma")),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit20.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# 21. The same, with the counting error of the predictor: me() declares a latent true log count
fit_x2 <- brm(
  log_gfap ~ DPI_f + me(log_pos, sd_log_pos),
  data = cell_data, prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b"), prior(normal(6, 3), class = "Intercept"),
                              prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma")),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 123, iter = 8000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 12), refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit21.rds", file_refit = "never"
)
slope_x1 <- as_draws_df(fit_x1)$b_log_pos
slope_x2 <- as_draws_df(fit_x2)$bsp_melog_possd_log_pos
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms: me()

```{r}
# The slope is the bsp_ coefficient of the me() term
summary(fit_x2)
```

### lm

```{r}
# The frequentist version without the error (ordinary least squares)
summary(lm(log_gfap ~ DPI_f + log_pos, data = cell_data))
```
:::

The reliability of the log count at the same day is `r round(reliab, 3)`: `r round(100 * (1 - reliab), 1)`% of its variance is counting error. With that figure an attenuation of about `r round(100 * (1 - reliab), 1)`% is what the theory expects, and what the models say is a slope of `r qs(slope_x1, 2)` when the count is treated as exact and `r qs(slope_x2, 2)` with `me()`. They agree, and for the same reason as before: the animals differ in their counts by far more than the counting error of any one of them. A predictor measured with a reliability of 0.99 is, for practical purposes, measured without error, and the exercise is useful because it tells you *when you may stop worrying*. If the reliability were 0.6, as can happen with a subjective score or with an assay run once on a noisy plate, the same exercise would say that the slope that you see is a part of the one that exists.

::: {.callout-tip title="Frequentist equivalent"}
The frequentist tools for an error in a predictor are regression calibration and SIMEX, in the packages `mecor` [@nab2021] and `simex` [@simex]. Neither is installed in this project, so I did not run them, and I will not describe their output. Both take the same ingredient as `me()`, the variance of the measurement error, and correct the slope by the reliability. The Bayesian version differs in that it propagates the uncertainty of the correction into the interval, instead of applying it afterwards.
:::

Use them to compute the reliability of a count from the replicates, compare it with the Poisson counting error of the figure above, and run me() with the error variance estimated from the replicates. -->

### Values below a limit of detection, which I can explain but not demonstrate {#sec-mdme-lod}

The first-class case of a hidden value on the *low* side is a measurement below the limit of detection of an assay: an ELISA concentration below the lowest standard, a band too faint on the film, a qPCR reaction whose Ct is "undetermined". The practice that I see most often is to replace the value by half the limit (or by the limit divided by $\sqrt{2}$) and carry on. The books that this one follows are of one voice against it: it creates a spike of identical values that did not exist, shrinks the spread, and distorts the slopes and the correlations [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. The alternative is the one that you already know from the wire: a [left-censored]{.ix ix="left-censored"} observation is a value that is *at most* the limit, and it contributes to the likelihood the probability of being below it, $F(\text{limit}\mid\mu,\sigma)$. In `brms` the only change is the left side of the formula, and `cens = "left"`.

<!-- PENDING-DATA: Daniel has ELISA data somewhere (to add later). Replace the illustration below with a real left-censored analysis, compared with substituting half the limit. -->

I have no real dataset with detection limits in this book, and I do not simulate one; the chunk below shows the syntax and is **not run**. It is an illustration with invented names (`conc`, `lod`, `below`), nothing more.

```{r}
#| label: lod-illustration
#| eval: false

# ILLUSTRATION, NOT RUN: a concentration with a detection limit (invented column names).
# For each row, `conc` is the measured value, or the limit itself when the value was below it;
# `below` is "left" when the value was below the limit and "none" otherwise
brm(
  log(conc) | cens(below) ~ group + (1 | animal),
  data = elisa, family = gaussian(),
  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b"), prior(exponential(1), class = "sigma"))
)
```

## An NA, a zero and a value below detection {#sec-mdme-td79}

I left for the end a case that I find the best teaching example in the book, because it is a single animal. In @sec-eda-missing-data I met animal `Td79` (three days after ischemia) because its `Pdgfrb_Neg` is missing, and I showed that its `Pdgfrb_Total` equals its `Pdgfrb_Pos` (398), which means that whoever computed the total treated the missing count as zero. There are two more things in that row. Its `PdgfrbLow_Intensity` is exactly 0, the only zero of that column. And the value that is missing is a *count of negative cells*, which is something that can be zero.

```{r}
#| label: td79-rules

# The rule that the file obeys everywhere else: positives plus negatives equal the total
chk_neg <- cell_data[!is.na(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg), ]
rule_holds <- all(chk_neg$Pdgfrb_Pos + chk_neg$Pdgfrb_Neg == chk_neg$Pdgfrb_Total)

# A DECISION, CONFIRMED AS A WORKING READING BY DANIEL: the negatives are the total minus the positives,
# which is zero for Td79 (it has no PDGFR-beta-negative cells)
cell_data$neg_rec <- cell_data$Pdgfrb_Total - cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos
cell_data$neg_100 <- cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg / 100
cell_data$neg_rec_100 <- cell_data$neg_rec / 100
td <- cell_data[cell_data$MouseID == "Td79", ]
stopifnot(rule_holds, td$neg_rec == 0, sum(is.na(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg)) == 1)
others_d3 <- cell_data[cell_data$DPI == 3 & cell_data$MouseID != "Td79", ]
```

The rule `Pos + Neg = Total` holds in all of the `r nrow(chk_neg)` animals with a recorded `Pdgfrb_Neg`. For `Td79`, applying it backwards gives `Pdgfrb_Neg` equal to `r td$neg_rec`, which is a very specific claim: *this animal has no PDGFR-β-negative cells in the section*. I asked, and the answer is that it may very well be the case. I take it as a working reading, not as a fact, and I say why it is not obviously safe: the other `r nrow(others_d3)` animals of the same day have between `r min(others_d3$Pdgfrb_Neg)` and `r max(others_d3$Pdgfrb_Neg)` negative cells, and no animal in the whole file has fewer than `r min(chk_neg$Pdgfrb_Neg)`. A section with 398 positive cells and none negative would be an unusual section, and it is worth checking on the image. Under that reading, the `NA` is not missing at all: it is a *structural* value that can be reconstructed from the other columns, and nobody should impute it. Under the other reading (the negatives were not counted, and the total is wrong), it is a missing count, and the imputation of @sec-eda-missing-data is the right treatment. The data cannot tell the two apart; the images can.

Then there is the intensity. `PdgfrbLow_Intensity` is `r td$PdgfrbLow_Intensity` for `Td79`, and it is the only zero in a column whose other values go from `r round(min(cell_data$PdgfrbLow_Intensity[cell_data$PdgfrbLow_Intensity > 0]), 1)` to `r round(max(cell_data$PdgfrbLow_Intensity), 1)`. It is tempting to read it as a measurement below a detection limit (a very faint signal), and it is not: the column is the intensity of the "low" class of PDGFR-β, and if that class has no cells there is nothing to measure. A zero here is not a faint value. It is, at best, a sum over an empty set, and at worst an undefined mean, written as zero by a script that did not know what else to write. The column tracks the number of negative cells closely (a correlation of `r round(cor(cell_data$PdgfrbLow_Intensity, cell_data$Pdgfrb_Neg, use = "complete.obs"), 2)`), which suggests that it accumulates over the cells of the class, but I cannot tell from the file whether it is a sum or a mean. If it is a mean, the zero should be an `NA`. @tbl-mdme_three shows the three things next to each other.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_three
#| tbl-cap: "An NA, a zero and a value below detection are three different things. The first two are the two values of animal Td79; the third is the case of the left-censored value that the chapter explains and does not demonstrate."

# What each of the three is, how to recognize it, and what to do
three <- data.frame(
  Value = c("NA in Pdgfrb_Neg", "0 in PdgfrbLow_Intensity", "Below the detection limit"),
  `What it says` = c("The count was not recorded, or it is a zero that was left blank",
                     "The class has no cells; the intensity is a sum over nothing, or an undefined mean",
                     "A measurement exists and is at most the limit"),
  `How to recognize it` = c("A rule the file obeys everywhere else (Pos + Neg = Total) reconstructs it",
                            "It sits at a count of zero in the column it depends on; it is the only zero in a column of positives",
                            "It is reported as the limit, as zero, or as a flag by the instrument"),
  `What to do` = c("Reconstruct it if the rule holds, and check the image; impute only if it cannot be reconstructed",
                   "Treat as undefined (NA) if the column is a mean; keep as zero if it is a sum; do not treat as a limit",
                   "Censor it at the limit; never replace it with half of the limit"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(three)
```

I want to test whether the decision matters on a model that the book has already shown. The model of @sec-eda-missing-data asks whether the count of negative cells says something about the count of positive ones, at the same day, and it handled `Td79` four ways: dropping it, imputing it inside the model with `mi()`, multiple imputation with `mice`, and plugging in extreme values. Now there is a fifth, which is to set it to its reconstructed value of zero. The models and priors are those of that chapter, so I read the first two from its cache and fit the others here.

```{r}
#| label: fit-td79

# The cached fits of the earlier chapter: complete cases (fit1) and the joint model with mi() (fit2)
fit_cc <- readRDS("models/eda-missing-data_fit1.rds")
fit_mi <- readRDS("models/eda-missing-data_fit2.rds")

# 22. The reconstructed value: Td79 has zero negative cells (same model and default priors as the earlier chapter)
cell_data$log_pos <- log(cell_data$Pdgfrb_Pos)
fit_t1 <- brm(
  log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_rec_100,
  data = cell_data, seed = 123, refresh = 0,
  file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit22.rds", file_refit = "never"
)

# Multiple imputation of the earlier chapter (20 completed datasets, normal model, Rubin's rules)
imp <- mice(cell_data[, c("log_pos", "DPI_f", "neg_100")], m = 20, method = c("", "", "norm"), seed = 123, printFlag = FALSE)
pooled <- summary(pool(with(imp, lm(log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_100))), conf.int = TRUE)
b_mice <- pooled[pooled$term == "neg_100", ]

# The reconstructed value in a frequentist fit
lm_rec <- lm(log_pos ~ DPI_f + neg_rec_100, data = cell_data)
b_lm <- c(coef(lm_rec)["neg_rec_100"], confint(lm_rec)["neg_rec_100", ])
```

::: panel-tabset
### brms

```{r}
# Reconstructed value (Td79 has zero negative cells)
summary(fit_t1)
```

### lm

```{r}
# The same by least squares
summary(lm_rec)
```

### mice

```{r}
# The multiple-imputation alternative, pooled with Rubin's rules
pooled
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-mdme_td79
#| fig-cap: "Coefficient for the number of negative cells (per 100 cells, on the log scale of the PDGFR-beta-positive count) under four treatments of animal Td79: dropped, imputed inside the model with mi(), multiple imputation with mice, and reconstructed as zero (total minus positive). Points are posterior medians or estimates and bars are 95% intervals."
#| fig-alt: "A forest plot with four rows. All four points sit close to 0.04 to 0.06 per 100 negative cells, and all four intervals cross zero, from about minus 0.03 to about 0.13. The reconstructed row has a slightly different position and a slightly narrower interval than the dropped row."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| warning: false

# Coefficient of the negative count under each treatment
cf <- function(fit, nm) fixef(fit)[nm, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]
td_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(label = "Dropped (complete cases)", t(cf(fit_cc, "neg_100"))),
  data.frame(label = "Imputed inside the model, mi()", t(cf(fit_mi, grep("mineg_100", rownames(fixef(fit_mi)), value = TRUE)))),
  data.frame(label = "Multiple imputation, mice", Estimate = b_mice$estimate, Q2.5 = b_mice$`2.5 %`, Q97.5 = b_mice$`97.5 %`),
  data.frame(label = "Reconstructed as zero (total minus positive)", t(cf(fit_t1, "neg_rec_100")))
)
td_df$label <- factor(td_df$label, levels = rev(td_df$label))

# Interval plot, one row per treatment
ggplot(td_df, aes(x = Estimate, y = label, xmin = Q2.5, xmax = Q97.5)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.55, linewidth = 0.9, color = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = "Coefficient per 100 negative cells (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11))
```

In @fig-mdme_td79 the four treatments give the same answer, `r round(td_df$Estimate[4], 3)` with the reconstructed value against `r round(td_df$Estimate[1], 3)` dropping the animal, which is what one animal in 49 should do. I should not leave the figure without saying what it hides. The imputation of @sec-eda-missing-data guessed about `r round(median(as_draws_df(fit_mi)[[grep("^Ymi_", names(as_draws_df(fit_mi)), value = TRUE)[1]]]) * 100)` negative cells for this animal, with an interval that went below zero, and the reconstruction says zero. Both are far apart as *values*, and they lead to the same slope because one animal contributes little to a slope. A model-based guess is a guess about a value that the file already contains, in a form that is not an NA. The lesson is the order of the questions: *can the value be reconstructed from the data?* comes before *how should it be imputed?*

```{r}
#| label: fit-td79-intensity

# 23 and 24. The zero intensity: the day-3 mean of PdgfrbLow_Intensity with Td79 as a zero, and without it
fit_i1 <- brm(PdgfrbLow_Intensity ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data, seed = 123, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit23.rds", file_refit = "never")
fit_i2 <- brm(PdgfrbLow_Intensity ~ DPI_f, data = cell_data[cell_data$MouseID != "Td79", ], seed = 123, refresh = 0,
              file = "models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit24.rds", file_refit = "never")
day3 <- function(fit) { d <- as_draws_df(fit); d$b_Intercept + d$b_DPI_f3 }
```

The zero intensity does matter more, because it is on a variable that is not tied to the count by an identity. The mean of the low-class intensity at day 3 is `r qs(day3(fit_i1), 1)` with `Td79` as a zero and `r qs(day3(fit_i2), 1)` without it (a Gaussian model for the intensity on the days, default priors): the zero pulls the day-3 mean down by `r round(median(day3(fit_i2)) - median(day3(fit_i1)), 1)` units (`r round(100 * (median(day3(fit_i2)) - median(day3(fit_i1))) / median(day3(fit_i2)))`% of the mean), with an interval that is already wide, since only eight animals contribute to it. That is not enough to change a conclusion that is a ratio of days, and it is the right size to show you what the choice costs: one value, written as zero, moves a group mean by about a seventh of its value.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Results.** One animal (`Td79`, day 3) had no recorded count of PDGFR-β-negative cells; its total equalled its count of positive cells, and I took its negative count to be zero (total minus positive), a reading that is consistent with the file and awaits confirmation on the image. The coefficient of the count of negative cells (log of the count of positive cells per 100 negative cells) was `r round(td_df$Estimate[4], 2)` (95% credible interval `r round(td_df$Q2.5[4], 2)` to `r round(td_df$Q97.5[4], 2)`) with that value, and `r round(td_df$Estimate[1], 2)` (`r round(td_df$Q2.5[1], 2)` to `r round(td_df$Q97.5[1], 2)`) when the animal was excluded. The intensity of the low class (0 in this animal, undefined if the class has no cells) was excluded from the analysis of its day-3 mean.

**Methods.** A missing count was reconstructed from the identity positive + negative = total, which held in all 48 animals with a recorded count. Results were compared with exclusion, imputation within the model (`mi()` in `brms`) and multiple imputation (`mice`, 20 imputations, Rubin's rules).
:::

## Missing predictors, and imputation as estimation {#sec-mdme-predictors}

The animal `Td79` was a missing *predictor*, and a missing predictor is the case in which the machinery of imputation earns its keep, because a model cannot simply drop what it needs to condition on without paying in rows. The idea that this chapter adds to @sec-eda-missing-data is a change of what we call it. In the Bayesian framework a missing value is not a hole to be filled before the analysis, it is an **unknown, and an unknown is a parameter**: it gets a prior (here, a sub-model for the variable that has gaps) and a posterior, estimated jointly with everything else [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020]. The imputed values are then not "data" that the analysis treats as known, they carry their uncertainty into every other parameter, and that is the whole difference with plugging in a mean.

The practical comparison with multiple imputation is shorter than it sounds. Multiple imputation (`mice`) draws several completed datasets from a model for the variable with gaps, fits the analysis on each, and pools with Rubin's rules [@mice]; `mi()` does the draw at every iteration of the sampler, inside the model. Both assume the loss is missing at random given what is in the imputation model, and the pitfall that I will repeat because it is the commonest one is that **the imputation model must include the outcome**: a model that imputes $x$ without looking at $y$ is assuming that they are unrelated, and it flattens the slope toward zero [@harrell2015; @mcelreath2020]. Both of mine did include it (the `mice` call has `log_pos` in the data, and `mi()` is fitted jointly with the outcome).

When there are *many* missing values in several predictors, which I do not have in the book, the syntax grows to one sub-model per incomplete variable. I show it in a chunk that is not run, with invented names, so that you can see the shape of it, and I would be glad to replace it with a real dataset if you have one with missing covariates.

```{r}
#| label: mi-illustration
#| eval: false

# ILLUSTRATION, NOT RUN: two incomplete predictors, each with its own sub-model (invented names).
# Every row keeps its place; the missing x1 and x2 are estimated as parameters, jointly with the outcome
brm(
  bf(y ~ mi(x1) + mi(x2) + group + (1 | animal)) +
    bf(x1 | mi() ~ group) +
    bf(x2 | mi() ~ group + mi(x1)) +
    set_rescor(FALSE),
  data = dat, family = gaussian()
)
```

`mi()` works only with continuous variables, because Stan cannot sample discrete parameters, so a missing count has to be handled as continuous or integrated out [@mcelreath2020], and when the loss is not at random the sub-model has to be extended with a model of the missingness itself, or replaced by a sensitivity analysis as in @sec-mdme-tipping.

## Checks, and how much the priors matter {#sec-mdme-checks}

I held every `brms` model of the chapter to the three thresholds of the book (R-hat below 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes above 400, no divergent transitions). @tbl-mdme_mcmc has the worst case of each fit and the time it took on four chains of this machine.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_mcmc
#| tbl-cap: "Sampler checks for the models of the chapter: worst R-hat, smallest bulk and tail effective sample sizes, divergent transitions, and the wall-clock minutes of the slowest chain."

# Worst-case diagnostics of every brms fit of the chapter
source("functions/mcmc_check.R")
fits_all <- list(
  "Wire: Gaussian, completed" = fit_w1, "Wire: Student-t, completed" = fit_w2, "Wire: capped entered as 60 s" = fit_w3,
  "Wire: censored (main)" = fit_w4, "Wire: falls censored at fall" = fit_w5, "Wire: falls as cap" = fit_w6,
  "Wire: 60 s crossings censored" = fit_w7, "Wire: censored, narrow priors" = fit_w8, "Wire: censored, wide priors" = fit_w9,
  "Wire: not completed (logistic)" = fit_w10,
  "Open field day 1: 270 s rule" = fit_o1, "Open field day 1: all sessions" = fit_o2,
  "NeuN cortex: all sections" = fit_s1, "NeuN cortex: sections 1 to 6" = fit_s2, "NeuN cortex: without 3 mice" = fit_s3,
  "Fiber tracts: log density" = fit_e1, "Fiber tracts: se()" = fit_e2, "Fiber tracts: counts, offset" = fit_e3,
  "Fiber tracts: se() and sigma ~ hemisphere" = fit_e4,
  "GFAP on PDGFR-b count: exact" = fit_x1, "GFAP on PDGFR-b count: me()" = fit_x2,
  "Td79 reconstructed as zero" = fit_t1, "Low intensity with Td79" = fit_i1, "Low intensity without Td79" = fit_i2
)
chk <- mcmc_check(fits_all)
chk$minutes <- sapply(fits_all, function(f) round(max(rowSums(rstan::get_elapsed_time(f$fit))) / 60, 1))
chk$max_rhat <- round(chk$max_rhat, 3); chk$min_ess_bulk <- round(chk$min_ess_bulk); chk$min_ess_tail <- round(chk$min_ess_tail)
knitr::kable(chk, row.names = FALSE)
```

All `r nrow(chk)` models are in the table, and `r sum(chk$ok)` of them pass all three checks. The smallest effective sample size of all the fits is `r min(chk$min_ess_bulk)` for the bulk and `r min(chk$min_ess_tail)` for the tail. The slowest models are the censored Student-*t* fits, about a minute each on four chains, and the `se()` and `me()` fits (the last has a latent value for each of the 49 animals), which I ran with more iterations and a higher `adapt_delta` after a first run showed an effective sample size below 400 or a few divergent transitions; two of the fits still report a single transition that reached the maximum tree depth, which costs time and not validity. The fits of the wire are the ones whose results I would most want you to check for yourself, so they are cached (`models/missing-data-measurement-error_fit*.rds`) and a re-render does not run them again.

The second check is about the priors of the censored model, and it is the one that matters most for this chapter, because the part of the likelihood that comes from the capped attempts depends on the *shape of the tail*, which the data cannot inform. I refit with a narrower and a wider set of priors for the coefficients, the spread between mice and the degrees of freedom of the Student-*t* (@tbl-mdme_prior_sens).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_prior_sens
#| tbl-cap: "Prior sensitivity of the censored model of the wire: ratio of typical crossing times (knockout to control), ratio per day of training, spread between mice and degrees of freedom of the Student-t, under the priors of the chapter, a narrower set and a wider set."

# The key quantities under the three sets of priors
ps_row <- function(fit, label) {
  d <- as_draws_df(fit)
  data.frame(Priors = label, `Ratio KO/control` = qs(exp(d$b_genotypeKO), 2), `Ratio per day` = qs(exp(d$b_day_c), 2),
             `SD between mice` = qs(d$sd_mouse__Intercept, 2), `Degrees of freedom` = qs(d$nu, 1), check.names = FALSE)
}
prior_tab <- rbind(
  ps_row(fit_w8, "Narrow: b N(0, 0.25), sd Exp(6), nu Gamma(2, 0.2)"),
  ps_row(fit_w4, "Chapter: b N(0, 0.5), sd Exp(3), nu Gamma(2, 0.1)"),
  ps_row(fit_w9, "Wide: b N(0, 1), sd Exp(1), nu Gamma(2, 0.05)")
)
knitr::kable(prior_tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

I read @tbl-mdme_prior_sens for what moves. The ratio of crossing times, the number that the chapter reports, moves by `r round(max(sapply(list(fit_w8, fit_w4, fit_w9), function(f) median(exp(as_draws_df(f)$b_genotypeKO)))) - min(sapply(list(fit_w8, fit_w4, fit_w9), function(f) median(exp(as_draws_df(f)$b_genotypeKO)))), 2)` between the narrowest and the widest set, a small fraction of the width of its interval; the narrow prior pulls the genotype coefficient toward zero, as a narrow prior should, and the intervals overlap almost completely. The degrees of freedom of the Student-*t* are what the data inform the least (the tail beyond 60 seconds is exactly where there are no data) and they are low under every prior, which is itself a statement that the attempts are heavy-tailed, so I would not report them without the prior next to them. The practical conclusion is the one a reader should need: the comparison of crossing times does not depend on the prior within this range, and the tail itself is an assumption.

## One table of decisions {#sec-mdme-decisions}

@tbl-mdme_decisions collects every case of the chapter, which of the three jars it belongs to, what I did and what the sensitivity analysis showed. I find this table, more than any model, to be the product of the chapter: a record that someone else could check and disagree with.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mdme_decisions
#| tbl-cap: "Every missing, hidden or blurred value of the chapter: what kind of absence it is, what I did with it and what the check showed."

# One row per case
dec <- data.frame(
  Case = c("Attempts that reached the 60 s cap", "Falls before the cap", "Two crossings at exactly 60 s",
           "Open-field sessions tracked under 270 s", "Animals with no session after day 1 (or day 15)",
           "NeuN sections after the sixth", "NeuN sections lost inside a series", "NeuN regions with zero positive cells",
           "Counting error of NeuN counts", "NA in Pdgfrb_Neg of Td79", "Zero in PdgfrbLow_Intensity of Td79"),
  Kind = c("Hidden (right-censored)", "A different event", "Hidden or exact (boundary)",
           "Absent in part", "Absent (loss of the animal)",
           "Absent, structural (the series ends)", "Absent, plausibly related to the tissue", "Structural, or a failed detection",
           "Blurred", "Absent or structural zero", "Undefined, not a limit"),
  `What I did` = c("Censored likelihood at 60 s (`cens()`)", "Left out of the time model; counted; two bracketing sensitivity analyses",
                   "Kept as exact times; refit as censored",
                   "Used what was seen (all sessions) and a tipping-point analysis on the kept ones",
                   "Model with a level for the animal (valid if the loss depends on the observed day-1 value); not tested further",
                   "Used what exists; refit on sections 1 to 6", "Used what exists; refit without the three mice",
                   "Not entered as zero counts in a log model; read each in context", "`se()` and a count model with an area offset",
                   "Reconstructed (total minus positive); compared with drop, `mi()` and `mice`", "Excluded from a day-3 mean; flagged"),
  `What the check showed` = c("Ratio of times larger than with dropping or replacing; the censored interval is wider",
                              "Ratio between the two extremes of the sensitivity analyses", "No change",
                              "Lost sessions had lower center share; the day-1 jump does not tip but shrinks",
                              "The three animals that leave were in the top third of day-1 shares (n = 3)",
                              "Not related to the injury (also in day-0 mice)", "All from ischemic days; no change in the ratio",
                              "Three kinds of zero; two regions to check on the image",
                              "Small next to the spread; no change in the estimates", "Same slope under four treatments",
                              "Moves a group mean by about a seventh"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(dec)
```

## What to write in a paper {#sec-mdme-report}

Three of the "How to report it" blocks above are the ones I would paste into a Results section: the censored comparison of crossing times, the tipping-point analysis of the open field, and the animal whose value was reconstructed. There is a fourth sentence that is easy to forget, and it is the one that a reviewer is most likely to want: *what was missing, why, and what was assumed*. I would put it in Methods, once, for the whole study.

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Methods.** Of `r n_att` attempts on the hanging wire, `r end_tab["WT", "Reached the cap"] + end_tab["KO", "Reached the cap"]` reached the 60-second limit and were treated as right-censored, and `r sum(attempts$end == "Fell")` ended in a fall and were analyzed separately. Of `r n_of_sess` open-field sessions in the `r n_of_an` animals analyzed, `r n_short` had fewer than 270 s of tracking; they were excluded from the main analysis and examined in a sensitivity analysis on the log-odds scale of the center share, and `r length(leavers)` animals had no session after day 1 or day 15 (attributed to postoperative mortality). For the NeuN counts, `r n_end` sections after the sixth were not available for `r length(unique(sec_grid$mouse[sec_grid$status == "Series ends before it"]))` mice and `r n_lost_in` sections were lost inside a series; the comparison of hemispheres was unchanged when they were excluded. Counting error (Poisson) accounted for less than `r ceiling(max(err_tab$"Variance due to counting (%)"))`% of the variance between sections in every structure. Missing data were assumed to be missing at random given the group, the day and the animal's earlier values, except where a sensitivity analysis is reported.
:::

## What the chapter leaves behind {#sec-mdme-close}

We started with three mice at 60 seconds and a question, and what I hope you take is a habit more than a model. Before touching any code, ask which of three things has happened: the value is *absent*, *hidden behind a limit* or *blurred*. An absent value asks for a reason and an honest statement of what the analysis assumes, and, when the assumption cannot be checked, a sensitivity analysis that turns it into a number you can move. A hidden value asks to stay in the model with what we know about it, which is that it is beyond a limit, instead of being dropped, replaced by the limit or replaced by half of it. A blurred value asks to be put next to the variation that matters and, if it is not negligible, to be carried by the model. And a zero, an NA and a value below detection are three different things, which a single animal in a table of 49 was enough to show.

The result about the wire was that dropping the capped attempts made the knockout delay look about `r round(100 * (median(ratio_ko) - 1)) - round(100 * (median(exp(dr_w$w2$b_genotypeKO)) - 1))` percentage points smaller than the censored model says, and the open-field result was that the inherited rule makes the day-1 jump look larger than it is, by an amount that does not reverse it. Two small things in opposite directions, from the same cause, which is that the values that are easiest to lose are the ones that matter. The books I have used agree on this: the question is never whether to take the missing values seriously, but which of the three jars they come from [@mcelreath2020; @gelman2020; @harrell2015].

Two topics are left outside on purpose. The first is time-to-event analysis proper, with hazards, competing risks and frailty models, which is the natural next step from the Kaplan-Meier curve of @fig-mdme_km and has its own place in the appendix on what comes next (@sec-appendix-next). The second is the question of what a statistic *means* when the cause of the missing values is part of the story, which is what the next chapter, @sec-causal-inference-splines, takes up with the tools of causal inference: a diagram of what causes the loss is exactly what tells you whether the loss is ignorable.
